articles.title: 'You can be believed and understood': Joanne Young speaks after verdict
articles.summary: Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, urged other victims of similar crimes to come forward.
articles.body:
A woman who was drugged by her husband and secretly advertised for sex on the internet has said if people "recognised their own experience" after this trial, "you're not alone and there are people who will believe you".

Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, spoke outside of Winchester Court and encouraged people to speak out against violence against women and girls.

Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing Young in the first trial of its kind in the UK.

Philip Young, 50, already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

articles.summary: The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
articles.body:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.

articles.title: VÍDEO: mulher é presa após tentar furtar 20 peças de roupa em loja | G1
articles.standfirst: Suspeita, de 60 anos, foi flagrada pelas câmeras de segurança do estabelecimento na manhã desta quinta-feira (19) em São José do Rio Preto (SP). Segundo a GCM, ela tem passagens pelo mesmo crime.
articles.summary: Uma mulher de 60 anos foi presa em flagrante na manhã desta quinta-feira (19) por furtar 20 peças de roupa de uma loja no Calçadão de São José do Rio Preto (SP).
articles.body:
Uma mulher de 60 anos foi presa em flagrante na manhã desta quinta-feira (19) por furtar 20 peças de roupa de uma loja no Calçadão de São José do Rio Preto (SP).

Segundo a Guarda Civil Municipal (GCM), não é a primeira vez que a suspeita é presa pelo mesmo crime. A equipe foi acionada por funcionários do estabelecimento depois que a mulher foi flagrada em uma situação suspeita pelo sistema de monitoramento de câmeras. Veja o vídeo acima.

Mulher foi presa furtando peças de roupas em São José do Rio Preto (SP) — Foto: Reprodução / Câmera de segurança

Na imagem, é possível ver que a investigada escolhe e separa as 20 peças as quais foram furtadas. Ainda conforme a GCM, os agentes abordaram a suspeita nas dependências do local e recuperaram as roupas em uma sacola.

Mulher é presa após tentar furtar 20 peças de roupa em loja de Rio Preto — Foto: Guarda Civil Municipal/Reprodução

Durante a consulta ao sistema de antecedentes criminais, os guardas municipais constataram que ela já possuía passagens anteriores por furto.

A suspeita foi levada à Central de Flagrantes de Rio Preto, onde permaneceu presa. A identidade da mulher não foi divulgada pela GCM até a última atualização desta reportagem.

articles.title: Usada por Trump na campanha, YMCA é tocada durante visita à China | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente americano assistiu à apresentação ao lado do chinês, Xi Jinping. Cena ocorreu horas depois de reunião inédita feita pelos dois com o russo Vladimir Putin.
articles.summary: Presidente americano assistiu à apresentação ao lado do chinês, Xi Jinping. Cena ocorreu horas depois de reunião inédita feita pelos dois com o russo Vladimir Putin.
articles.body:
Usada por Donald Trump na campanha presidencial nos Estados Unidos, a música YMCA, do grupo Village People, foi usada em uma apresentação ao presidente durante visita à China.

Nesta quinta-feira, Donald Trump e o presidente chinês, Xi Jinping, assistiram a uma apresentação musical em que os bailarinos dançaram ao som da canção. Veja a cena:

A cena ocorreu horas depois da reunião feita por Trump e Xi com o presidente da Rússia, Vladimir Putin. Inédito, o encontro trilateral registrou a primeira conversa, cara a cara, entre os três líderes (leia mais abaixo) .

Os presidentes dos EUA, Rússia e China se encontraram em Shenzhen. Anfitrião, o líder chinês defendeu um "mundo livre de armas nucleares", e afirmou que elas "devem ser completamente proibidas e destruídas".

O presidente da Rússia, Vladimir Putin, o presidente da China, Xi Jinping, e o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, chegam para uma reunião trilateral na Villa Kylin, em 19 de novembro de 2026, em Shenzhen, na China. — Foto: Win McNamee / Reuters

O encontro começou às 5h30 e terminou cerca de 7h do horário de Brasília. Uma hora após o fim, os três países divulgaram uma declaração de paz conjunta, se comprometendo com um diálogo sobre riscos nucleares e concordando que uma guerra nuclear nunca deve acontecer.

Quando a reunião começou, Trump exaltou os companheiros e falou da importância do encontro entre eles. O presidente americano também voltou a fazer críticas ao Tribunal Penal Internacional, dizendo que a corte está "fora de controle" - Putin tem um mandado de prisão expedido contra ele por crimes de guerra.

"Os três têm responsabilidades especiais. Nossos três países estão em uma posição única para discutir a redução de armas nucleares. Falaremos sobre todos os problemas que estão sendo discutidos no mundo", afirmou.

Putin, que está em guerra com a Ucrânia há quase cinco anos, também iniciou suas declarações falando em "manutenção da paz e segurança", e adotou um discurso conciliador:

"Nossos três estados têm responsabilidade conjunta na manutenção da paz e da segurança. Devemos discutir os laços globais e regionais, bem como a segurança energética. Rússia, China e Estados Unidos podem contribuir para o fortalecimento da estabilidade global se cooperarem de forma construtiva".

Xi também fez uma defesa da paz e disse que Estados Unidos, China e Rússia "devem ser parceiros e amigos":

"Os principais países devem se respeitar mutuamente e coexistir pacificamente. Nossos três países devem abandonar a mentalidade da Guerra Fria. As grandes potências não devem interferir nos limites uma da outra em questões sensíveis. Devemos respeitar a soberania, a integridade territorial e os interesses fundamentais".

articles.title: De resíduos a combustível: a tecnologia da 3Di para o biometano | G1
articles.standfirst: Com origem em Foz do Iguaçu, empresa desenvolve soluções para a produção de biometano e amplia sua presença no mercado latino-americano.
articles.summary: Com origem em Foz do Iguaçu, empresa desenvolve soluções para a produção de biometano e amplia sua presença no mercado latino-americano.
articles.body:
O que acontece com os resíduos orgânicos depois que deixam de ser aproveitados? Em diferentes atividades produtivas, materiais que antes representavam um desafio para o descarte passaram a despertar o interesse de um setor em expansão. Isso porque, em condições adequadas, sua decomposição pode gerar biogás, um recurso energético que ganha cada vez mais espaço nas discussões sobre sustentabilidade e transição energética.

O potencial desse gás, porém, depende da tecnologia utilizada para seu aproveitamento. É nesse processo que atua a 3Di Biogás , empresa brasileira especializada no desenvolvimento de equipamentos capazes de purificar o biogás e transformá-lo em biometano, um combustível renovável que pode substituir o gás natural em diferentes aplicações.

Com sede em Foz do Iguaçu, no Paraná, a empresa nasceu da aproximação entre o conhecimento acadêmico e as necessidades do setor produtivo. Sua trajetória começou em uma incubadora vinculada ao Itaipu Parquetec, ambiente voltado ao desenvolvimento de soluções inovadoras. A partir das primeiras demandas do mercado, a 3Di passou a desenvolver tecnologias próprias para o tratamento e a purificação do biogás.

Hoje, a empresa é referência nacional em seu segmento e amplia sua atuação para acompanhar o crescimento de um mercado que encontra novas oportunidades dentro e fora do Brasil.

A tecnologia por trás de um combustível renovável

Para compreender a importância desse trabalho, é preciso conhecer uma etapa fundamental da produção de biometano. O biogás gerado pela decomposição de matéria orgânica contém metano, mas também outras substâncias que precisam ser removidas para que ele alcance as características necessárias ao uso como combustível.

É justamente essa transformação que a 3Di Biogás torna possível. Por meio de processos de purificação, o gás passa por um tratamento que eleva sua qualidade até atingir os padrões exigidos para o biometano.

O resultado é um biocombustível 100% renovável, com características semelhantes às do gás natural e potencial para abastecer veículos ou atender às necessidades energéticas de indústrias.

Com soluções desenvolvidas para diferentes demandas, a 3Di atende tanto empresas que já trabalham com biogás quanto negócios interessados em começar a aproveitar esse recurso. A proposta é oferecer tecnologia capaz de acompanhar as necessidades de cada operação e contribuir para ampliar o uso de combustíveis renováveis.

A experiência construída no Brasil também abriu caminho para uma nova fase. Há aproximadamente dois anos, a 3Di Biogás passou a integrar uma estrutura global, movimento que fortaleceu suas perspectivas de expansão internacional.

A América Latina ocupa uma posição estratégica nesse processo. Além do mercado brasileiro, a empresa identifica oportunidades em países como o Paraguai, Argentina, Chile e Colômbia, onde o desenvolvimento de novos projetos pode impulsionar a demanda por equipamentos especializados.

A expansão acompanha uma mudança importante no setor energético. À medida que mais empresas buscam alternativas aos combustíveis fósseis, cresce também a necessidade de tecnologias capazes de viabilizar a produção de biometano em escala comercial.

Para a 3Di , esse cenário representa a oportunidade de participar desde as primeiras etapas de novos empreendimentos, levando sua experiência tecnológica a mercados que começam a explorar o potencial do biogás.

Novo projeto amplia a capacidade tecnológica

Profissionais equipados com EPIs acompanham os trabalhos em altura na estrutura metálica da planta industrial. — Foto: Divulgação/3DI Biogás.

Entre os projetos que marcam essa fase está o desenvolvimento de um equipamento de grande porte, atualmente em etapa de finalização. A solução foi projetada para atender a uma usina do setor sucroenergético e será utilizada em uma biorrefinaria.

O equipamento permitirá processar grandes volumes de biogás, realizando a purificação necessária para sua conversão em biometano. A iniciativa representa um avanço na capacidade de desenvolvimento da empresa, especialmente para operações industriais de maior escala.

Da incubadora tecnológica aos projetos de grande porte, a trajetória da 3Di Biogás acompanha a evolução de um setor que ganha relevância na matriz energética. Com investimentos em desenvolvimento tecnológico e perspectivas de expansão, a empresa busca contribuir para que o potencial do biogás se transforme em novas oportunidades de geração e aproveitamento de energia renovável.

articles.standfirst: As principais rodovias da região devem receber 343 mil veículos durante o feriado prolongado, celebrado na sexta-feira (20). Movimentação começa nesta quinta (19).
articles.summary: O feriado da Consciência Negra deve atrair 343 mil veículos às rodovias de Piracicaba, com picos de tráfego a partir desta quinta-feira e reforço na segurança viária.
articles.body:
Dia da Consciência Negra: veja horários de pico nas rodovias e rodoviárias da região de Piracicaba — Foto: Divulgação/Via Colinas

As principais rodovias da região de Piracicaba (SP) devem receber 339 mil veículos durante o feriado do Dia Nacional de Zumbi e da Consciência Negra, celebrado na sexta-feira (20). O movimento começa nesta quinta (19) e segue até segunda (23). As rodoviárias de Piracicaba e Limeira (SP) também esperam aumento no número de passageiros.

A concessionária Eixo SP, responsável pelas rodovias Geraldo de Barros (SP-304), Hermínio Petrin (SP-308), Irineu Penteado (SP-191) e Washington Luís (SP-310), prevê a passagem de 155 mil veículos entre a tarde de quinta-feira (19) e a tarde de domingo (22), no retorno do feriado, no sentido da capital.

Segundo a concessionária, os horários de maior movimento serão:

Para melhorar o tráfego, a empresa suspendeu obras e intervenções que possam causar lentidão. Apenas serviços emergenciais serão mantidos. A medida vale desta quinta-feira (19), após as 12h, até segunda-feira (23), às 12h.

Na concessionária Rodovias do Tietê, a previsão é de 73 mil veículos na Rodovia Comendador Mário Dedini (SP-308), conhecida como Rodovia do Açúcar. Já a Rodovia Jornalista Francisco Aguirre Proença (SP-101) deve receber 44 mil veículos.

A concessionária informou que terá guinchos e ambulâncias distribuídos ao longo das rodovias para atender motoristas em emergências.

A Via Colinas prevê a passagem de 67 mil veículos pelo trecho da SP-127, formado pelas rodovias Fausto Santomauro, Cornélio Pires e Antônio Romano Schincariol. A via passa por Piracicaba, Saltinho (SP) e Rio das Pedras (SP).

Segundo a concessionária, os horários de pico serão:

Veja as recomendações para os motoristas:

fazer a manutenção do veículo antes da viagem;

verificar se os documentos do veículo e do condutor estão em dia;

ultrapassar apenas em locais permitidos;

parar no acostamento só em caso de emergência.

Antes de pegar a estrada, o motorista deve checar itens como nível de óleo e de água, calibragem dos pneus, alinhamento, balanceamento e o funcionamento dos freios, das luzes e da sinalização.

Frota de ônibus em Piracicaba — Foto: Divulgação/Prefeitura municipal de Piracicaba

Cerca de 35 mil pessoas devem passar pela Rodoviária de Piracicaba durante o feriado prolongado, segundo estimativa da Associação Piracicabana das Empresas de Auto Ônibus (Apeao). O movimento deve começar na quinta-feira e seguir até domingo, na volta do feriado.

Os destinos mais procurados são a capital paulista, cidades do interior, o litoral de São Paulo, municípios do estado do Rio de Janeiro, cidades do interior do Paraná, Curitiba e Belo Horizonte.

Para evitar contratempos, a administração orienta os passageiros a:

chegar ao terminal com pelo menos 30 minutos de antecedência;

conferir a empresa de ônibus, o horário e o local de embarque;

levar documento oficial de identificação original, inclusive das crianças.

Menores de 16 anos devem viajar acompanhados dos pais ou responsáveis. Se o adolescente for viajar sozinho, será necessário apresentar autorização assinada por pelo menos um dos pais ou pelo responsável legal, com firma reconhecida.

Segundo levantamento da Secretaria de Transportes e Mobilidade Urbana de Limeira, feito com as empresas que operam no terminal, o fluxo de passageiros na Rodoviária de Limeira deve aumentar durante o feriado.

O maior movimento deve ocorrer entre quinta-feira (19) e se estender durante o final de semana até a volta do feriado.

Os destinos mais procurados são cidades como Campinas e São Paulo, além de Marília, Assis, Tupã, Araraquara, São José do Rio Preto, Curitiba, Londrina, Florianópolis, Goiânia e Brasília.

A administração recomenda que os passageiros comprem as passagens com antecedência e cheguem mais cedo ao terminal para evitar filas e imprevistos.

articles.title: Trump, Xi e Putin passam ao largo do multilateralismo | G1
articles.standfirst: Triunvirato de presidentes ensaia uma declaração de paz que ignora conflitos, esvazia o TPI e reforça interesses próprios.
articles.summary: Triunvirato de presidentes ensaia uma declaração de paz que ignora conflitos, esvazia o TPI e reforça interesses próprios.
articles.body:
Com agendas tão conflitantes, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping e Vladimir Putin, representantes de três dos cinco membros permanentes do Conselho de Segurança , arriscaram uma “declaração de paz” que passa ao largo da defesa do multilateralismo .

Os três foram vagos quanto ao empenho para a reforma da ONU, mas fizeram questão de minar a atuação do Tribunal Penal Internacional , que expediu um mandado de captura para o presidente da Rússia por crimes de guerra.

“Os três chefes de Estado reconheceram que o princípio do consentimento do Estado e o respeito pela imunidade dos funcionários do Estado são de suma importância e concordaram que o Tribunal Penal Internacional e outros órgãos similares não devem abusar de sua jurisdição”, diz um dos quatro pontos do documento divulgado após a reunião em Shenzhen.

Os presidentes de EUA, China e Rússia esbanjaram cordialidade em gestos, mas reforçaram seus interesses nos próprios termos. Não causa surpresa, portanto, que o comunicado final tenha omitido as guerras na Ucrânia e no Irã ou os limites da inteligência artificial.

Depois da conversa de uma hora e 20 minutos, apenas Putin falou , mas para assegurar que não negociará com a Ucrânia sobre o fim da guerra que se arrasta há quase cinco anos: “Após os ataques à Ponte da Crimeia, não negociaremos. Responderemos a esses ataques. E quero que todos saibam disso".

Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping e Donald Trump chegando para reunião trilateral — Foto: Win McNamee/Pool via REUTERS

Putin, aliás, saiu triunfante de um encontro marcado por simbolismos . Retornou em grande estilo à mesa de negociações, após ser ostracizado do cenário internacional, e alçou a Rússia ao mesmo patamar das duas superpotências .

Ele foi descrito por Trump como um amigo , enquanto a mídia estatal russa exibia a imagem de um de seus assessores portando uma mala que conteria os códigos nucleares da Rússia .

Como anfitrião, Xi parece ter obtido uma vitória importante — a de se impor como um influente ator diplomático nesse novo formato geopolítico, sem a predominância dos EUA, além de fortalecer internamente a sua imagem.

Do ponto de vista concreto, o triunvirato esboçou apenas o olhar individual para os temas de interesses comuns, excluindo dele a Europa e outros parceiros.

Em Berlim, outros líderes e representantes de 40 países estão reunidos nesta quinta-feira na chamada “Coalizão de Dispostos” justamente para apoiar a Ucrânia.

No ocaso da popularidade, Trump buscou se aferrar ao simbolismo da imagem produzida pelo encontro trilateral, vangloriando-se por estar ao lado de Xi e Putin. Tantos elogios provocaram a reação irônica do premiê da Polônia, Donald Tusk: “Deus, proteja-nos de tais amigos!” , escreveu no X.

articles.title: Mianmar cometeu genocídio contra os muçulmanos rohingya, diz ONU | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão da Corte Internacional de Justiça afirma que as ações do governo do país, em 2017, tiveram a "intenção de destruir" uma parte substancial da população minoritária e fala em compensação com indenizações.
articles.summary: Decisão da Corte Internacional de Justiça afirma que as ações do governo do país, em 2017, tiveram a "intenção de destruir" uma parte substancial da população minoritária.
articles.body:
O mais alto tribunal das Organizações das Nações Unidas ( ONU ) decidiu, nesta quinta-feira (19), que os milhares de assassinatos e a violência sexual generalizada perpetrados pelas forças de segurança de Mianmar contra a minoria muçulmana Rohingya em 2017 configuram genocídio patrocinado pelo Estado.

De acordo com a Corte Internacional de Justiça, as ações do governo do país tiveram a "intenção de destruir" uma parte substancial da população minoritária.

"O tribunal considera que as forças de segurança de Myanmar mataram milhares de civis rohingya, perpetraram atos generalizados de violência sexual, bem como atos de extrema violência contra crianças e atacaram rohingya em fuga. Com base em todas as evidências reunidas, o Tribunal entende que a única inferência razoável que pode explicar as ações de Mianmar é a intenção de destruir uma parte substancial da população Rohingya no norte do estado de Rakhine", disse o presidente da corte, Yuji Iwasawa.

O Tribunal Internacional de Justiça ( TIJ ) profere sua sentença no caso apresentado pela Gâmbia, que acusa Myanmar de genocídio contra a minoria muçulmana Rohingya — Foto: REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw

Após a sentença, o painel de 15 juízes também afirmou que Mianmar tem a obrigação de compensar os Rohingya pelas violações cometidas e que indenizações serão determinadas posteriormente.

Além disso, a corte determinou que o país deve permitir o "retorno seguro e digno aos seus locais de residência e a reunificação das famílias dos rohingya deslocados em consequência dos atos ilícitos".

A decisão do tribunal é definitiva e não pode ser contestada. O governo de Mianmar não respondeu a um pedido de comentário da agência de notícias Reuters.

Mianmar é acusada de realizar 'limpeza étnica' contra minoria Rohingya — Foto: Darren Whiteside/Reuters

Foi a primeira vez que o tribunal responsabilizou um Estado por genocídio , que raramente foi comprovado em tribunais internacionais, principalmente porque os promotores precisam provar uma intenção específica de destruir, total ou parcialmente, um grupo nacional, étnico, racial ou religioso.

A decisão, tomada sete anos após a ação ter sido movida pela Gâmbia, país de maioria muçulmana, marcou apenas a quarta vez desde o Holocausto nazista que um tribunal internacional considerou que o limiar legal para comprovar genocídio havia sido atingido.

O ministro da Justiça da Gâmbia disse que a sentença é "uma vitória para a comunidade" e mandou recado para os rohingya: "Eles sobreviveram. Eles testemunharam. E hoje, eles acreditarão".

Um líder dos refugiados rohingya em Bangladesh, Sayed Ullah, expressou sua "mais profunda gratidão" em pronunciamento à agência de notícias AFP:

"Expressamos nossa mais profunda gratidão a Bangladesh, Gâmbia e à OCI (Organização de Cooperação Islâmica) que estiveram conosco durante todos esses anos. Pedimos a todos que continuem conosco até que possamos retornar para casa".

articles.title: Steakhouse warning: How to tell if you're getting the cut of beef you actually paid for
articles.summary: New York strip, rib-eye and filet mignon make up the "holy trinity" of steak cuts, but experts say most diners struggle to tell them apart.
articles.body: Ordering steak at a restaurant isn't always cut and dry. With different cuts, grades and preparations to consider, it's easy to get something other than what you expected — or even other than what you're paying for. An Illinois man recently went viral after calling out Texas Roadhouse for serving him a cheaper sirloin instead of a filet mignon on three separate visits. The chain only confirmed one incident and said management corrected it, but the episode struck a nerve online: many people realized they wouldn't even know the difference between the two. EXPERTS REVEAL HOW TO SPOT FAKE 'WAGYU' SO YOU DON'T GET RIPPED OFF ON PREMIUM BEEF Experts shared with Fox News Digital what diners should expect from popular steak cuts, how to decode menu terms and what to ask their server. Filet, rib-eye or New York strip? Katie Flannery, a third-generation butcher at Northern California's Flannery Beef, calls filet, rib-eye and New York strip the "holy trinity" of steak cuts. Choosing among them comes down to what a diner wants most. Filet mignon is a good choice for tenderness because it comes from a muscle that gets little use. It has less inherent flavor than other popular cuts and is usually the most expensive, in part because only a small amount comes from each animal. For a beefier flavor, Flannery recommends rib-eye. MEAT EXPERT SHARES THE MISTAKE MOST AMERICANS MAKE WHEN COOKING STEAK "Just know it'll have a little bit more chew than a filet," she said. John Tesar, executive chef of Palladino's Steak & Seafood in New York City and Dallas, describes the rib-eye as having a tender center and a more flavorful, sturdier outer section. "You get a tender inner circle and a sturdier, more flavorful outside, all supported by fat," he said. A New York strip, meanwhile, is recognizable by the band of fat along one side and has a heartier texture. Flannery said it has less flavor than a rib-eye and, depending on its grade, can have more chew than a filet. That leaves the porterhouse, which includes both a New York strip and a filet on one bone and is often large enough to share. AMERICA'S PRESIDENTS AND THEIR STEAKS: HOW PERSONAL TASTE SHAPED THE OVAL OFFICE Some menu terms can make it all more confusing, experts noted. A "sirloin filet" may be sirloin shaped to look like filet mignon. Sirloin comes from the more-used hip and rump, making it less tender than filet. What grades and aging mean The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) grades offer another clue and reflect a steak's marbling, or flecks of fat within the muscle, which contributes to flavor and tenderness. The main grades are Prime, the top grade, Choice and Select. Filet, rib-eye, New York strip and sirloin can all come from Prime, Choice or Select beef. The USDA grades the carcass, so cuts from that carcass share its grade, according to the agency. Grading is voluntary, so some beef is ungraded. Flannery said about 10% of graded cattle earn the Prime designation, while about 70% qualify as Choice. Prime has more marbling than Choice or Select. WHY HOMEMADE PRIME RIB CAN BE 'EVEN BETTER' THAN AT A STEAKHOUSE, EXPERTS SAY "Fat is flavor, honestly," she said. More marbling can contribute to flavor and tenderness, but it is only one factor. "The more the muscle moved in the animal's lifetime, the tougher it is," Flannery said. Both wet- and dry-aging can improve tenderness, while dry-aging concentrates flavor, Flannery said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Wet-aging is common, so seeing it on a menu isn't necessarily a special selling point, Flannery said. "Pretty much everybody does wet-aging," she said. The beef is vacuum-sealed and refrigerated as it ages, avoiding the weight loss that comes with dry-aging, when meat is exposed to air in a cooler. What to ask your server Steaks can vary in appearance, but certain features offer clues. Tesar said filet mignon is typically thick and round, while a rib-eye has a distinctive outer section called the rib cap, or spinalis. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Raw steaks can offer more clues for consumers, Flannery said: filet has finer muscle fibers, while sirloin's grain is more visible. But sirloin can be cut into a rounded "baseball" shape that resembles filet mignon, making the two cuts easy to mix up. Still, it can be difficult for diners to identify a cut once it's sliced or slathered in a sauce or toppings. Chef Luis Haro, vice president of culinary innovation at Logan's Roadhouse, said a whole steak is easier to recognize by its shape. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "When the steak is served whole, it's usually easier because you can look at its shape," he said. If a menu description is unclear, diners can ask their server what cut they're ordering and what to expect. If a steak appears different from what someone ordered, Tesar suggested asking politely: "I thought this was a certain steak, and I am not familiar with the way you are presenting it. Can you explain that to me?" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If the server can't clarify, diners can ask for the chef or manager, he said.

articles.title: Trump claims Iran is developing bioweapons: Is there any evidence?
articles.summary: Trump threatens to ‘wipe out’ Iran in case of attack as Tehran’s capabilities remain unclear.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has accused Iran of exploring chemical and biological weapons, reigniting allegations that Tehran may be planning a “dirty bomb” attack.

Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Trump said Iran was “looking at gases, looking at bio”, without providing evidence to support his claims.

Trump claimed Tehran has pivoted away from developing nuclear capabilities given that “we’ve shut them out”. “We’ll see what happens after January 1,” he said, before referring to Iranians as “nasty people”.

His comments follow a report by CNN on Tuesday citing US intelligence indicating that Iran may be developing plans to target senior officials in Trump’s administration with a chemical weapon in Washington, DC.

On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed concerns about a possible Iranian attack, saying the US does not face an “imminent threat”. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed Rubio’s conclusion, confirming there was no indication of an upcoming attack.

But Trump did not dismiss the possibility. Asked whether people in Washington, DC, should be concerned about a potential attack, Trump said he did not believe so, but threatened retaliation if it happened.

“If it does happen, we wipe them out,” he said.

Is there evidence that Iran possesses a ‘dirty bomb’?

Iran is a signatory to the Biological Weapons Convention, but it ratified it six years before the 1979 revolution that overthrew the Pahlavi monarchy and established the Islamic Republic of Iran. It is also a party to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), ratified in 1997.

Nonetheless, Western intelligence agencies have long maintained that Iran is pursuing unconventional capabilities.

According to a report by a British think tank, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), Iran’s biological weapons programme is believed to have accelerated since the Iran-Iraq War, which ended in 1988.

After Iraq extensively used chemical weapons during that conflict, Tehran resolved never again to accept such an asymmetry in unconventional capabilities, RUSI concluded. What followed was a sustained effort to develop biological agents under the cover of civilian research.

Hamish de Bretton-Gordon, an analyst and former British Army officer, said it would not be surprising if Iran was resorting to developing chemical weapons after US military strikes on its nuclear facilities set back its nuclear programme.

“It is also possible they are looking at biological weapons,” de Bretton-Gordon told Al Jazeera. “With the advent of AI-enabled bio weapons, they have the potential to be as devastating as nuclear weapons at a fraction of the cost and time.”

Such weapons could “replace their nuclear programme [and] be far more difficult to detect”, he added.

According to Dan Kaszeta, an associate fellow at RUSI focussing on defence against chemical, biological and radiological weapons, “this is an area where things are incredibly vague”.

“Any country with the industry, science and laboratory infrastructure that Iran has could, in theory, make chemical and biological hazards in sufficient quantity for a singular incident like a localised terrorist attack,” Kaszeta told Al Jazeera. “The underlying technology is not highly sophisticated.”

“As far as whether Iran has had a chemical or biological weapons programme has been debated for decades, ever since the Iran-Iraq war,” he added. “There have been arguments put forward on both sides of that hypothesis, without any firm conclusion.”

Jacek Siewiera, nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Europe Center, separated scientific expertise operational weapons capability from the political willingness to conduct an attack.

“A research programme does not, by itself, establish the ability to carry out a particular operation abroad,” Siewiera told Al Jazeera. “A credible assessment would require corroborated information about capability, operational reach and intent. I would therefore be cautious about assigning a probability to the specific scenario described.”

This is not the first time the US has accused an enemy of possessing unconventional weapons.

Glen Rangwala, associate professor in the Department of Politics and International Studies at the University of Cambridge, in the UK, said: “There is a fairly extensive history of successive US administrations making unfounded allegations about countries of the Middle East possessing weapons of mass destruction (WMD).”

“It serves to raise the stakes internationally and put potential domestic critics on the back foot,” Rangwala told Al Jazeera.

Washington launched an invasion of Iraq in 2003 after claiming that Saddam Hussein’s government posed an imminent threat due to its alleged chemical, biological and nuclear programmes.

A Senate committee found the CIA and others in George W Bush’s administration manipulated evidence to justify the occupation of Iraq, calling the operation a “whitewash for the White House.”

No stockpiles of banned weapons, nor evidence of a programme to develop any, were ever found in Iraq following the US-led military action.

Rangwala said this tendency to level accusations against rivals has been matched by “an extensive history of successive US administrations not acknowledging how some of its allies in the Middle East have or host WMD”.

“There are good reasons to be concerned about proliferation, but not only on one side of the balance,” he added.

images.caption: Trump says Iran is 'looking at gases, looking at bio', without providing evidence to support his claims [File: Bonnie Cash/EPA]

articles.title: What is a ‘nuclear briefcase’, spotted at the APEC summit?
articles.summary: Vladimir Putin’s special briefcase – thought to carry access to nuclear weapons – made a rare appearance in Shenzhen.
articles.body:
As the leaders of the United States, China and Russia arrived in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Thursday, one man in Russian military uniform was spotted carrying a mysterious black briefcase.

As a Russian state television camera zoomed in on the naval officer travelling with President Vladimir Putin, reporter Yevgeny Popov gestured towards the case, telling viewers, “this is the nuclear briefcase”. The officer smiled and confirmed it was indeed the bag carrying the Russian president’s direct access to his country’s nuclear arsenal – known as the “Cheget”.

The US president has an equivalent satchel, known as the “nuclear football”, which routinely travels with him, though it has yet to be spotted in Shenzhen. Whether Chinese President Xi Jinping travels with a similar case is unclear.

So are these briefcases simply symbols to project power, or do they really give leaders the ability to order a nuclear strike at a moment’s notice?

It is a specially kitted-out briefcase that connects to the military command system, through which a leader can order a nuclear attack.

The US and Russian (then-Soviet) systems emerged during the Cold War, when the leaders of both powers faced the prospect of having to make decisions about nuclear strikes with little warning.

However, the image of a finger hovering over a red button is somewhat far-fetched. Military personnel and a much larger communications system are required to carry out a leader’s order.

How do the US ‘football’ and Russia’s Cheget differ?

The origins of the nuclear briefcase in the US, known as the “nuclear football”, predate the 1962 Cuban missile crisis. Historians trace it to Dwight Eisenhower’s administration, and a declassified memo indicating that Eisenhower briefed John F Kennedy on the device the day before Kennedy took office in January 1961.

The US president also carries a card nicknamed the “biscuit”, which contains codes used to verify the president’s identity when issuing a nuclear order. The vice president has access to a “backup football” and authentication codes in case he or she needs to assume presidential authority.

The Congressional Research Service states that the US president alone can authorise the use of nuclear weapons but can seek advice from senior military leaders.

Russia’s version of the briefcase, the Cheget, takes its name from a mountain in the Caucasus. It entered Soviet service in 1983 and a naval officer traditionally carries the president’s case for him. In 2015, the Yeltsin Center in Yekaterinburg put the briefcase used by Boris Yeltsin, Russia’s first post-Soviet president, on display.

Today’s Cheget links the president to the Russian military’s central command, and it can transmit an order to use nuclear weapons, but it cannot launch them. Russia is believed to have three such briefcases, assigned to the president, the defence minister and the chief of the General Staff.

Under Russia’s published nuclear doctrine, the president decides whether to use nuclear weapons. The Cheget communicates through Russia’s “Kazbek” command-and-control network, which supports a separate communications system called “Kavkaz”. Public accounts differ on how many of the briefcases would be needed to authenticate a presidential order.

In theory, a nuclear attack could begin while a president is on a plane, at a summit or asleep in a hotel.

Nuclear briefcases, therefore, allow attacks or counterattacks to be launched at any time, regardless of the leader’s location. That matters in terms of deterrence: the idea that an adversary may decide against attacking if they believe the other side could still retaliate.

As the economist and strategist Thomas Schelling wrote in his 1966 book Arms and Influence: “The power to hurt is bargaining power.”

Russian media also showed Putin accompanied by naval officers carrying briefcases on a visit to Beijing in 2023. At a summit, the sight of the Cheget can serve as a visible reminder of Russia’s nuclear arsenal. The Shenzhen footage establishes that the case is there, which also acts as a strong reminder that Russia possesses nuclear weapons.

“The fact that Kremlin-backed TV channels showed this tells us a lot,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. “This is pure political theatre and a symbolic performance of a man that is conscious his country’s standing in the world is not what it once was.”

“Compared to the United States or China, Russia does not have the military or economic capacity it once did – this is an attempt to performatively demonstrate that Russia belongs at that grand table.”

Do other countries have nuclear briefcases?

The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute counts nine nuclear-armed states. The US and Russian briefcases are the best documented. Elsewhere, governments have generally revealed more about who can authorise the use of nuclear weapons than about what equipment travels with their leaders.

In the United Kingdom, only the prime minister can authorise the use of nuclear weapons, according to the House of Commons Library. Each new prime minister also writes four handwritten “letters of last resort” – one for the commander of each nuclear-armed submarine – setting out what to do if a nuclear attack destroys the government.

Meanwhile in France, that authority rests with the president. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Nicolas Sarkozy handed over the nuclear codes to Francois Hollande when he left office in 2012.

China maintains a “no first use” policy, meaning Beijing says it would deploy nuclear weapons only in response to a nuclear attack from another country. Whether President Xi Jinping travels with a dedicated nuclear briefcase remains unclear.

The government in India says only the Political Council of its Nuclear Command Authority, chaired by the prime minister, can authorise the use of nuclear weapons, while it remains unclear whether it carries equipment.

Pakistan and North Korea also have nuclear weapons, while Israel is widely believed to hold them, but there is not enough reliable public information to know whether their leaders travel with comparable cases.

(Al Jazeera)

articles.title: Home of Bangladesh’s former leader Muhammad Yunus set on fire
articles.summary: The blaze broke out during heightened violence before ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s planned return.
articles.body:
The ancestral home of the former interim leader of Bangladesh and Nobel Peace Prize winner, Muhammad Yunus , was set on fire in the port city of Chittagong, police have said.

The fire broke out before midnight on Wednesday in the city, about 300km (185 miles) southeast of the capital, Dhaka, authorities said on Thursday.

The arson was followed by protests by supporters of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Thursday, as violence swept parts of the country.

Yunus served as interim leader of the country for 18 months after a mass uprising forced Hasina to quit. She was flown out of the country by the military on August 5, 2024.

An abandoned ground-floor room in Yunus’s house was set on fire, and a police patrol spotted it and immediately doused the flames, officer Mozammel Haque told local media.

It was not immediately clear who was behind the blaze.

“Criminals set fire to the eastern side of the house. The area was being used as a storeroom,” Chittagong Metropolitan Police spokesman Aminur Rashid said, adding there were no casualties.

Authorities are investigating, and additional details were not immediately available.

Yunus has faced hostility from supporters of Hasina’s Awami League party, which has since been banned.

Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, said 22 of its branches have been subject to arson attacks in the last few days. Police have also reported explosions of crude bombs and roadblocks in Dhaka and other locations throughout Bangladesh in recent weeks in advance of Hasina’s planned return.

The 79-year-old politician, who has been living in India since fleeing Bangladesh, announced she would return to the country in December despite facing a death sentence. She told The Associated Press news agency earlier this month that even death could not prevent her from returning to Bangladesh.

Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia last year after a court convicted her of crimes against humanity over the deadly 2024 crackdown on protesters. The government has rejected her request for a new passport and identity card that would allow her to return.

Thursday’s protests were held after a call by the Awami League for a national “lockdown” to mark the anniversary of Hasina’s sentencing last year.

Earlier this week, protesters set fire to a police station and the home of a lawmaker in Gopalganj.

Clashes there killed two members of the governing Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), police said on Thursday, adding that 107 arrests have been made since Wednesday.

articles.title: Takeaways from the Trump-Xi-Putin summit and ‘GTA VI’ launches to rave reviews: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Trump touts his friendships with China’s Xi and Russia’s Putin at a historic three-way summit.
articles.body: Trump touts his friendships with China’s Xi and Russia’s Putin at a historic three-way summit. Workers whose employers dropped GLP-1 coverage scramble to pay out-of-pocket costs. And the highly anticipated “GTA VI” goes on sale. Here’s what to know today. Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic summit President Donald Trump has wrapped up historic three-way talks with the leaders of U.S. rivals, Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. What these three men might decide has the potential to reverberate across the globe. But the spectacle of Trump’s meeting with Putin and Xi, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, may be what delivers the defining image. Sitting around the table were three of the world’s most powerful leaders: The U.S. with its largest economy, Russia its biggest nuclear arsenal, and China its largest standing army and manufacturing sector. “We are really making history,” Trump said before the talks began. Trump called Xi and Putin “friends,” but it was unclear what exactly had been accomplished during the 90-minute meeting. Still, comparisons have already been drawn with the Yalta Conference of 1945, in which President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin sat down to carve up the postwar world. Trump focused on calling for new curbs on nuclear weapons, after the last remaining nuclear treaty between Washington and Moscow lapsed this year, and China, whose arsenal is smaller than that of the other two, has resisted calls to be involved in a new one. The Russian leader said it was up to them to “strengthen the system of international law” (Russia has been accused of war crimes in Ukraine) as well as work on issues such as food and energy security. Xi meanwhile stuck to broader themes. Post-summit identical statements released by China and Russia — but not yet the U.S. — also called for the three countries to increase their energy production and supply, which would fuel Russia’s oil-driven war economy. As well as nuclear issues, the leaders said they would discuss Iran, economics and trade. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO’s remarks were made while he was in China as part of Trump’s delegation at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. “I’m not MAGA,” Musk said in an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.” Musk also said he expected Democrat Gina Hinojosa to be “quite moderate” when she takes office as Texas governor. articles.title: Trump’s heir, but not his echo: JD Vance, Iran and the limits of loyalty
articles.summary: When Donald Trump picked JD Vance as his running mate in 2024, he chose a politician who had once described him as “America’s Hitler”.
articles.body: When Donald Trump picked JD Vance as his running mate in 2024, he chose a politician who had once described him as “America’s Hitler”. Two years later, Vance is not only the US vice-president but is also frequently discussed as a possible successor to Trump and the Republican Party’s “America First” movement.The transformation has been striking. Vance has embraced much of Trump’s political agenda, from economic nationalism and restrictive immigration policies to scepticism towards America’s overseas commitments. Yet the war with Iran has demonstrated that the two men do not always share the same instincts on how that agenda should be pursued.Vance has generally been more sceptical of prolonged military involvement. He has also sought to place greater emphasis on the domestic and economic consequences of foreign policy. These differences do not necessarily amount to a break with Trumpism. But they offer an indication of how Vance might seek to define the movement if he eventually has to lead it without Trump.From critic to political heirVance’s transformation is central to understanding his relationship with Trump. In a report published in July 2024, Reuters recalled that Vance had publicly called Trump an “idiot” and described him as “reprehensible” during the 2016 presidential campaign. Reuters also reported that Vance had privately compared Trump to Adolf Hitler.By the time Trump selected him as his running mate in 2024, however, Vance had become one of his most prominent defenders. Reuters described the choice as a signal that Trump wanted his Make America Great Again (Maga) movement to continue beyond his own presidency. Vance was increasingly being viewed within the Republican Party as a possible inheritor of that political project.The ideological overlap is visible across several policy areas. Both men have challenged the traditional Republican preference for free trade, advocated tougher immigration enforcement and questioned the scale of America’s international commitments.For Vance, economic nationalism is also about the position of American workers. His criticism of multinational corporations and the movement of manufacturing overseas fits into the broader argument that the US should prioritise domestic industry over the interests of global markets. This is a central theme of Trump’s political appeal as well.Ukraine: a more pronounced scepticismForeign policy is where Vance’s views have, at times, been more clearly defined than Trump’s. Both have questioned the scale of American support for Ukraine and argued for an end to the war through negotiations. But Vance has been a more consistent and vocal opponent of continued US assistance.In an interview in 2022, Vance said: “I don't really care what happens to Ukraine one way or the other.” Reuters quoted the remark in its July 2024 assessment of his foreign-policy positions. The agency also reported that Vance had argued Ukraine had little chance of regaining all the territory occupied by Russia and that American resources should instead be directed towards issues such as the US-Mexico border and competition with China.Trump, too, has expressed scepticism about US aid to Kyiv and promised to end the conflict through negotiations. However, Reuters noted that, unlike Vance, Trump had not explicitly opposed the congressional aid package for Ukraine passed in April 2024.Their preference for a negotiated settlement may overlap, but Vance’s opposition to American involvement has been more categorical. It is therefore important not to treat their positions as identical.Vance’s wider scepticism towards overseas military commitments was also evident before he became vice-president. In a 2023 opinion article for The Wall Street Journal, he praised Trump for not starting wars during his first term. The Associated Press later cited Vance’s explanation for supporting Trump: “I know he won't recklessly send Americans to fight overseas.”Iran: Where the differences became visibleThe US-Israeli military campaign against Iran in February 2026 brought Vance’s foreign-policy instincts into sharper focus.Trump argued that military action was necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Vance supported that stated objective, but the president himself acknowledged that the two had approached the decision differently.At a news conference on March 9, Trump said Vance was “philosophically a little bit different than me” and had been “maybe less enthusiastic about going” to war. Trump added: “I felt it was something we had to do. I didn't feel we had a choice.” The remarks were reported by the Associated Press.Vance’s reservations had also been evident before the strikes. He had told The Washington Post that there was “no chance” the United States would become involved in a prolonged conflict similar to the Iraq war, Reuters and AP reported.Once the operation began, however, Vance publicly backed the president. In an interview with Fox News, he defended the administration’s approach by arguing that Trump had clearly defined the military objectives.“What's so different about this, Jesse, is that the president has clearly defined what he wants to accomplish,” Vance told Fox News, according to the Associated Press.Vance’s role in the conflict later extended to diplomacy. He became a central figure in efforts to negotiate an end to the fighting and defended the preliminary agreement reached with Tehran. In June, he presented the agreement as a success, pointing to its potential economic benefits, including lower fuel prices and the resumption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Trump publicly joked about the political risks of giving his vice-president responsibility for the negotiations. “If it works out, I'm going to take the credit. If it doesn't work out, I'm blaming JD,” Trump said on June 17, according to the Associated Press.The agreement did not bring a lasting end to the conflict. On November 2, Vance told reporters that he and Trump were optimistic about the prospects of a negotiated settlement. “We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more,” he said, as reported by CBS News. Trump had also indicated on Truth Social that a deal with Iran “could happen”.The position changed within days. On November 12, Trump said the United States did not need an agreement with Tehran and directed Vance to shift his attention from Iran to a domestic anti-fraud campaign.“We don't need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that the United States had “got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!” Reuters reported that the directive came after Vance had been involved in efforts to resolve the conflict.Beyond the immediate political fallout, the differences over Iran point to a broader debate within the Maga movement about the extent of America's military involvement overseas. Dr Ashok Sharma, a geopolitics expert and Visiting Fellow at the University of New South Wales Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy, said the disagreement reflected competing approaches to American foreign policy."The differences between Trump and JD Vance over the Iran war reflect a deeper ideological tension within the Maga movement. While Trump views military action against Iran as necessary to protect American strategic interests and prevent nuclear proliferation, Vance represents a more restrained, America First approach. He questions prolonged military engagements and their economic and political consequences", Sharma said.Israel: Support, but not without limitsVance’s position on Israel also requires a distinction between support for the country and agreement with every decision taken by its government.In July 2024, Reuters described Vance as a consistent supporter of Israel, a position broadly in line with Trump’s. Vance had also supported sending aid to Israel while opposing a wider package that included assistance to Ukraine.However, during the Iran conflict, Vance became more willing to question Israeli actions when he believed they could undermine American diplomatic objectives. In June 2026, he criticised Israeli strikes on civilian infrastructure in Beirut, suggesting that they risked damaging US-led peace efforts.Vance made the broader argument more explicitly in September, when he addressed the All-In Summit. “We cannot let our Middle Eastern foreign policy be subservient to the State of Israel,” he said, according to The Times of Israel.He also argued that Trump had shown a willingness to disagree with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when he believed American interests required it. Vance’s comments were not a rejection of the US-Israel relationship. Rather, they reflected his argument that Washington should retain the freedom to pursue its own strategic priorities.The midterm setbackThe clearest public divergence between Trump and Vance emerged after the Republican Party’s losses in the November 2026 midterm elections. Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress, and Vance identified the Iran war as one of the reasons for the defeat.In a post on X on November 4, Vance wrote: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.” He also challenged Republicans who believed the military operation had been worth the political cost.“If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote. CBS News reported that Vance identified four concerns among voters who had supported Trump in 2024 but switched to the Democrats: the Iran war, the cost of living and inflation, putting America first, and the US relationship with Israel.Trump continued to defend the decision to launch the war, arguing that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon justified the operation. In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, he acknowledged that Iran had been a factor in the election but said he had no regrets. “I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he said, according to The Guardian’s report of the interview.Trump did not entirely dismiss Vance’s assessment. The Associated Press reported that he described the vice-president’s post as “good” and said: “I know how he feels about it.” However, Trump continued to defend the military campaign.Vance's criticism of the Iran war has also raised questions about the political calculations behind his position. Prof Rajan Kumar, professor at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, told TOI that there could be multiple explanations, ranging from genuine disagreement over the war's consequences to an attempt by Vance to distinguish himself from a policy that may have hurt the Republican Party electorally."Vance may have raised the issue for two reasons. First, he genuinely believes that the Iran war was the principal reason behind the Republicans' defeat. Many within the party believe the conflict created a foreign-policy deadlock and contributed to domestic inflation through higher energy prices, hurting the Republicans in the midterm elections," Kumar said."The other explanation is political. If Vance is positioning himself as a potential Republican presidential candidate in 2028, he may feel the need to distance himself from a policy that contributed to the party's electoral setback and demonstrate that he does not agree with Trump on every issue," he added.Kumar said Vance's position could also be interpreted differently by those who view his political trajectory as evidence of opportunism. Vance had criticised Trump before joining his administration, subsequently aligned himself with the president, and is now publicly highlighting differences over the Iran war."Many Republicans felt that traditional conservative values were not being adequately represented by Trump. However, they remained silent because of his strong electoral support and the fear that he could back challengers against them in primary elections. A few did speak out, but Trump has a habit of eliminating his own loyalists, including his former vice-president Mike Pence and former secretary of state Mike Pompeo".The balancing actVance’s challenge is to distinguish himself from Trump without appearing to reject the movement that brought him to the vice-presidency. So far, his differences have largely been expressed through emphasis and approach rather than a wholesale break with the president.On economic nationalism and immigration, he remains broadly aligned with Trump. On Ukraine, his opposition to continued US assistance has been more pronounced. On Iran, he supported the administration’s stated military objective but was more cautious about the prospect of a prolonged conflict and later became a leading advocate of negotiations.The post-midterm disagreement, Sharma argued, raised a larger question about the direction of the Republican Party's foreign policy once Trump eventually leaves the political stage."The larger question is whether post-Trump Maga will continue Trump's assertive foreign policy or return to its original promise of avoiding costly overseas wars."For now, Vance’s political position rests on two competing requirements: Maintaining the support of Trump’s voters and demonstrating that he can offer something beyond a continuation of the president’s own political approach. Whether that balance is enough to make him the movement’s next leader remains to be seen.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Muir Mhòr offshore wind farm approved for site off Peterhead
articles.summary: The Scottish government says its consent comes with a number of conditions.
articles.body:
The Scottish government has approved plans for a 67-turbine floating offshore wind farm at a site about 39 miles (63km) from Peterhead in Aberdeenshire.

Developer Fred Olsen Seawind said its 1GW Muir Mhòr project could generate enough electricity annually for more than a million homes.

Generation could start in the early 2030s.

The Scottish government said its consent came with a number of conditions, including a requirement for measures to reduce potential impacts on fishing and seabirds.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Public Service Reform Secretary Ivan McKee said Muir Mhòr had "significant potential" to strengthen Scotland's energy security and create jobs.

He added: "Tackling climate change and reaching net zero is a key priority for the Scottish government, with renewable energy at the heart of this."

Martha Lovatt, senior development and consents manager for Muir Mhòr, said: "Today's decision is the culmination of years of intensive environmental assessments, technical work, and constructive engagement with local communities, marine stakeholders, and industry partners.

"Throughout this journey, we have listened carefully, taken all feedback on board, and designed a project that balances the need for renewable energy generation with genuine respect for our coastal and marine environment."

articles.title: ‘Groundbreaking’ Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Five key takeaways
articles.summary: Leaders hailed the unprecedented meeting as historic, with discussions spanning nuclear risks to energy flows.
articles.body:
The presidents of the United States, China and Russia have declared a shared intent to stabilise energy flows, prevent nuclear proliferation and find mechanisms to work more closely together, at an unprecedented summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday.

The meeting, held on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conclave, was the highlight of three days of intense diplomacy in the region, where leaders from multiple countries — including US President Donald Trump — had previously gathered in Manila for other summits.

Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired the summit with Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, after a series of bilateral meetings among the leaders.

At the end of a more than one-hour-long meeting, they released what they described as a “peace declaration”. They met at a time when multiple wars — including the US war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine — have taken a heavy toll on economies and people around the world.

Here are some key takeaways from their summit:

Trump said that the meeting was between “three of the world’s largest nations,” mentioning that the trio of countries also hold the planet’s three biggest nuclear arsenals. “We’re making history,” the US leader said in his opening remarks, referring to their trilateral summit.

The US president added that “too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” however, Trump noted, “No peace [was] ever forged by declining opportunities.”

All three leaders reiterated that it was up to them to protect the world.

China’s Xi said the countries should shed a “Cold War mentality” and become friends — something reiterated by Russia’s Putin, in his own words, adding that the three countries can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively.

After the meeting, the trio released a joint “peace declaration”.

Under the China-US-Russia “peace declaration”, the three countries have reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows, Chinese state media reported.

Global energy supplies have been on edge since the US attacked Iran in February this year, and Tehran closed down the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil supplies previously transited. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further compounded global energy woes.

But there appears to be no end to both wars — either by the US or Russia — and it remains unclear how the promise of stable energy flows will be realised given the different priorities of the three nations.

In fact, there was no reference to the war on Iran at the summit — other than Trump reiterating that Tehran cannot have a nuclear weapon. And a Kremlin spokesperson said that Ukraine was not even the “central topic” at the trilateral meeting, though it was a central part of Putin’s bilateral talks with Trump earlier. Trump also called on Xi to help out in resolving the war on Ukraine.

In a major statement before the trilateral meeting started, China’s Xi said, “Nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world.

“Nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought; every effort must be made to prevent it,” he added.

The thrust of that statement was also later adopted in the post-meeting joint declaration, with three countries pledging to hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation. The leaders also committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security at their trilateral meeting.

In his opening remarks at the meeting, the US president said that the “three countries are uniquely positioned to discuss nuclear weapons” — given they hold the biggest arsenals.

Trump also said Xi agreed with him that the Strait of Hormuz needs to stay open and that Iran must not be allowed to have nuclear weapons. Tehran has repeatedly said that its nuclear mission is for civilian purposes and that it holds no desire to build weapons.

As the US, Russia, and China sat down for the trilateral meeting to discuss a variety of issues, European leaders gathered nervously in Berlin, analysts say, at a meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.

The leaders of these three countries appeared to take it upon themselves to solve the conflicts and issues plaguing global economies.

Next month, President Trump is hosting the G20 Summit in Miami, Florida, and China’s Xi Jinping is almost certain to attend. But Russia too is a member of the G20.

President Putin has skipped recent summits of the grouping because of an International Criminal Court warrant against him for the Ukraine war, and because European members of the G20 have been clear that they do not want to share a room with him.

Trump, however, has invited Putin to attend the Miami G20. The US is not a part of the ICC, so it is under no obligation to arrest the Russian president.

“The discussion at the trilateral summit was very frank and helped the leaders to better understand one another,” Putin said after the meeting.

Is this the start of a G3? We shall know in the coming weeks.

Among the many points in the “peace declaration” agreed upon by Trump, Xi, and Putin in Shenzhen was a pointed critique of the International Criminal Court.

The three leaders demanded that the ICC and “similar institutions” not “abuse their positions”.

What is it about the ICC that upsets all three powers — none of whom are members of the court?

United States: The US has long had an adversarial relationship with the ICC, but those ties have grown especially tense in recent years after the court began investigating allegations of abuse by US soldiers in Afghanistan. The court’s warrant for the arrest of Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu on charges of having committed war crimes in Gaza caused a further rupture, and the US has now publicly, as part of official policy, made the dismemberment of the ICC a goal. It has imposed sanctions against the institutions and its officials.

Russia: Like the US, Russia has never trusted the ICC. But after the ICC issued an arrest warrant against President Putin on charges related to the Russian war on Ukraine, Moscow has become even more fiercely opposed to the UN court and its way of functioning.

China: There have been times in previous years when China — while never endorsing the court — has been lukewarm to it. But the spate of arrest warrants against leaders of sovereign nations, including Philippines ex-President Rodrigo Duterte, turned Beijing into a strident critic. The ICC has also received petitions from activists accusing China of committing genocide against the Uighur community in Xinjiang — an allegation Beijing rejects.

articles.title: South Korean court orders retrial for ex-PM Han over martial law attempt
articles.summary: The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court’s legal interpretation of insurrection.
articles.body:
South Korea’s Supreme Court has ⁠⁠overturned the 15-year prison sentence of former Prime ⁠⁠Minister Han Duck-soo for his role in the brief imposition of martial law two years ago, sending the case back ⁠⁠to a lower court.

A majority of justices found shortcomings in the lower court’s assessment of Han’s actions before former President Yoon Suk Yeol’s declaration, particularly his proposal to convene a Cabinet meeting that could have given legitimacy to the president’s decision.

The justices said it was difficult to establish whether Han had intended to undermine the Constitution, given the urgent circumstances at the time.

The special prosecution team for Han’s case said in a statement that they respect the ⁠⁠court’s ruling.

The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court’s legal interpretation.

In the aftermath of the imposition of martial law, former President Yoon was impeached and removed from office by the Constitutional Court in April 2025.

A presidential election two months later brought Lee Jae Myung to power.

Yoon’s 2024 decree plunged the country into chaos, but lasted only about six hours as opposition lawmakers scrambled to overturn the decision.

Han, 77, one of several top officials sentenced over the short-lived martial law bid , was handed a 23-year jail term in January for his involvement, which the court said threatened “the constitutional order” and amounted to insurrection.

An appeals court then reduced the sentence to 15 years in May, citing Han’s “more than 50 years as a public official prior to the martial law declaration”.

Han has denied wrongdoing in relation to ⁠⁠all charges except one for perjury. He said last year that while he regretted not being able to stop Yoon from declaring martial law, he “never agreed to it or tried to help”.

Yoon, meanwhile, has ⁠⁠denied wrongdoing and said he exercised his powers as president. He was convicted of insurrection in February and sentenced to life in ⁠⁠prison.

He has appealed and awaits that ruling, which ⁠⁠is scheduled for January.

articles.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
articles.summary: The US Secretary of Defence says Venezuela has "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner".
articles.body:
The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.

The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.

Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.

Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".

Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.

Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.

He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".

Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.

They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.

Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture , which they deny.

Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.

"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.

"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.

"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive Nicolás Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."

Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."

He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".

Rodríguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations".

"In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.

While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech Rodríguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".

In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".

From Venezuela, Hegseth travelled on to neighbouring Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration.

Colombia is already part of the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and in August, Hegseth had floated the possibility of joint US-Colombian military operations against armed groups.

In his post, he stressed that any decision would be taken while respecting Colombia's constitution, and the country's laws and sovereignty.
