articles.title: What the ICJ genocide ruling means for the Rohingya people
articles.summary: This is the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.
articles.body:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya minority ethnic group.

After seven years of deliberations, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa delivered the long-awaited ruling on Thursday in a verdict which took three hours to read out.

Nine of the 15-judge panel found that Myanmar has committed genocide, the court said. Justices also voted in favour of a landmark reparations order against the country which it says has persecuted the mostly Muslim group for decades.

It is the first time in the history of the World Court, which was established in 1945, that it has ruled that a state has committed genocide. The decision is final and cannot be appealed.

The Gambia brought the landmark case against Myanmar in 2019.

After many years of persecution, Myanmar’s military launched an offensive in 2017 which forced about 750,000 Rohingya from their homes and lands, and pushed them into squalid refugee camps, largely in neighbouring Bangladesh.

About 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the early stages of the military operation. Thousands of others died in shipwrecks as they fled on perilous boat trips across the Bay of Bengal. The Rohingya reported cases of mass killings, torture and rape at the hands of the Myanmar military and allied militias.

“This is a huge day for the Rohingya people and all people of Myanmar,” said Matthew Smith, a campaigner with the advocacy group Fortify Rights, who nervously stood in The Hague’s Peace Palace along with Rohingya survivors and the Gambian delegation, as the ruling was read out.

“People have waited for such a long time for this moment,” he said.

The ruling “will provide much-needed momentum to efforts to hold the perpetrators and architects of the genocide individually criminally accountable”, he added.

The lengthy ruling, delivered by ICJ judge Yuji Iwasawa of Japan, said that Myanmar’s security forces “killed thousands of Rohingya” in Rakhine State, committed widespread sexual violence against them as well as acts of “extreme violence against children”.

Villages were “systematically destroyed”, replaced with permanent structures and then re-settled by non-Rohingya, the ruling said. The military also “intentionally” caused “serious bodily and mental harm” to the group’s members, and high-ranking officials disseminated anti-Rohingya hate speeches that portrayed them as “subhuman and a violent threat”.

Those who fled their homes have had little or no opportunity to return because of the destruction of their homes, the court found, and acts against children in particular established the military’s intent to “prevent birth” in the group.

Furthermore, the Myanmar military knew that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians and allied militias participated in the military campaign against the Rohingya. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” Iwasawa said.

The ICJ ruled that Myanmar must cease all acts of violence and investigate those culpable. Myanmar must also take immediate and effective steps to investigate all persons suspected of culpability, prosecute and punish the guilty, and provide guarantees that this will never happen again.

Importantly, the court ruled that Myanmar must institute restitution and reparations in the case – something campaigners have long pushed for.

Restitution measures, the court said, should see Myanmar: allow and facilitate the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; return or replace all collective property damaged; facilitate the search for the disappeared and ensure proper burials; provide for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured and ensure their protection from persecution.

The court said it could not determine compensation but ordered Myanmar to submit a report within two years outlining a plan.

“This judgement is a landmark victory for the Rohingya people and for countless individuals in Myanmar who have endured violence at the hands of the military. It represents an important step toward accountability and honours the courage and perseverance of the victims and survivors who have spent years seeking justice,” Arsalan Suleman, partner at legal firm Foley Hoag and lead counsel for The Gambia, said after the verdict was delivered.

For the Rohingya people, this is the day they have long hoped for.

“The Rohingya hope to receive justice and enjoy safety both inside and outside Myanmar,” Kyaw Min Sabber, founder of Rohingya Human Rights Initiative, told Al Jazeera ahead of the ruling.

“They also hope that they will no longer face displacement and arbitrary killings in Rakhine State,” he said.

Can the ICJ compel Myanmar to comply with this ruling?

The ICJ cannot enforce its rulings, but they do carry weight: The Gambia could now table the case at the United Nations Security Council and request action.

This ruling is especially significant because the 1948 Genocide Convention requires proof of the specific intent to destroy – in whole or in part – a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. That requirement is notoriously difficult to prove, and has contributed to the ICJ never having held a state responsible for committing genocide.

In 2007, for example, the court ruled that Serbia violated the Convention by failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops in Srebrenica but that the state itself did not commit the act – even though UN tribunals found individuals culpable for genocide.

Thursday’s ruling could, therefore, have important implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza.

The Rohingya are a largely Muslim ethnic group based primarily in Myanmar’s western Rakhine State, which shares a border with Bangladesh.

Until their forced displacement in 2017, there were about 1.4 million Rohingya in Myanmar, making them a minority among Myanmar’s 137 ethnic groups. Other Rohingya populations live in India, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.

While the Rohingya identify as Indigenous to Myanmar – and have been present there for many generations – the government does not recognise them and maintains they are “illegal migrants” from Bangladesh. In 1982, authorities passed a citizenship law that essentially rendered most of the group’s population stateless. Successive governments, including the civilian-led administration of Aung San Suu Kyi that governed between 2016 and 2021, have continued to exclude the Rohingya.

The group has experienced waves of violence and displacement over the years. In 2013, the rebel Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) was formed. In late 2017, when ARSA attacked police posts, Myanmar’s armed forces, known as the Tatmadaw, launched a massive response operation. The Rohingya were subjected to unprecedented levels of violence: The military shot men dead, raped women, threw babies into fires and razed Rohingya villages, survivors said.

A UN fact-finding mission in 2019 concluded that the Tatmadaw gang-raped men, women and children, and committed “genocidal acts”.

The violence saw at least 740,000 Rohingya flee to Bangladesh in a span of months. About 1.2 million Rohingya now live in crowded conditions in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar, while about 520,000 remain in Myanmar under severe restrictions. Bangladesh wants them to return to Myanmar, and over the years, aid allocated for the Rohingya has shrunk, especially since United States President Donald Trump took office in January 2025 and slashed foreign aid spending.

In November 2019, the small West African nation of The Gambia took Myanmar to The Hague. The Gambia, itself a Muslim-majority country, was backed by the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and was itself just emerging from years of repression under the dictator Yahya Jammeh.

Its team of lawyers, led by then-Justice Minister Aboubacarr Tambadou, argued that Myanmar had committed genocide in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

Former leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi, who was later overthrown in a military coup in 2021, personally appeared at the court at the time and called The Gambia’s claims “incomplete and misleading”.

But in January 2020, the ICJ ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent a genocide of Rohingya, in what experts called a “stunning rebuke” to Suu Kyi.

Eleven countries – Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, the Maldives, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Slovenia, Ireland, Belgium, France and Britain – applied to support the case.

During hearing in January 2026, The Gambia, led by current Justice Minister Dawda A Jallow, reiterated that Myanmar’s ruling military “deliberately targeted” the Rohingya for “destruction” and that it acted with “genocidal intent”.

The Gambia asked the court to establish Myanmar’s obligation to provide reparations to Rohingya survivors, order its government to prosecute those responsible, and ensure the Rohingya can return safely .

Myanmar – now under military leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the crackdowns and later took power in the 2021 coup – denied the allegations, however, arguing that its military was forced to respond to armed attacks with its “clearance operations”.

Survivors and rights groups say the ruling is clear vindication after decades of suffering.

The verdict also provides legal backing for justice and accountability at the highest level that could see the Rohingya achieve their goal of returning safely and with dignity to their homes, and of being finally acknowledged by the state of Myanmar.

Smith said the statement on reparations is especially important and that the court’s ruling now gives the parties ground to negotiate the details.

“Reparations for the Rohingya must be comprehensive, meaningful, and shaped by Rohingya survivors themselves,” he said, adding that it must not be conflated with aid or humanitarian assistance and must come with official acknowledgement of wrongdoing.

The plan should include financial compensation for the immense losses suffered, restitution of confiscated land and property, restoration of citizenship and fundamental rights, and guarantees of safe return, medical care, trauma support, education, and livelihood opportunities, he said.

“No amount of money can undo a genocide, but meaningful reparations can help restore rights, dignity, and a measure of justice to people who have been denied all three for generations,” Smith added.

Can the Rohingya return safely to Myanmar?

This is very uncertain. Myanmar is in turmoil, prompting serious concerns about their safety there.

The overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in 2021 triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and has displaced more than 3.5 million.

Fighting between the army and the Arakan Army, a largely Buddhist rebel group also operating in the Rakhine State which also targets the Rohingya, has worsened conditions further.

In August, Myanmar said it had verified more than 300,000 refugees in Bangladesh and registered them for repatriation, but stated that this could only begin after security is restored in Rakhine.

Furthermore, while a genocide finding formally recognises the harm the Rohingya have suffered, it may do little for them in the short term, Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer, told Al Jazeera ahead of the ruling .

“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” he said.

All eyes are now on whether – or how – Myanmar will implement the ICJ’s rulings and submit the required report by its November 2028 deadline.

Survivors want states which support the Rohingya to keep up pressure on Myanmar’s military to ensure an end to ongoing rights violations by the army and the Arakan Army, Kyaw Min Sabber said.

The Gambia, the OIC, and all the countries which have supported the case “have an important responsibility to continue supporting the protection and pursuit of justice for the Rohingya people”, he said, including those refugees living in India, Malaysia, Thailand, Nepal and other countries where they face mistreatment, arbitrary detention, and the fear of deportation.

“Their commitment should extend beyond the court proceedings and continue until the Rohingya can safely return to Myanmar with full equal rights, security, and dignity,” he said.

articles.title: El-Sayed downplays antisemitism concerns over rhetoric, says people 'should be uncomfortable' over Gaza
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed dismissed fears that his criticism of Israel could potentially fuel more antisemitism when asked by The Atlantic.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed downplayed critics' concerns that his comments on Israel could fuel antisemitism during an interview with The Atlantic on Tuesday. El-Sayed discussed his views on Israel, including his accusations that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal and that Israel committed genocide during the war in Gaza. Staff writer Jonathan Lemire asked El-Sayed what he would say to people who believe these criticisms of Israel "fuel [their] fears of antisemitism." Though El-Sayed emphasized that he does not want to frighten people, he suggested that some of the concerns reflected "discomfort" rather than a threat to safety. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOST CONFRONTS ABDUL EL-SAYED ON HIS RESPONSE TO ATTACK ON JEWISH SYNAGOGUE "I'm sorry for your fear," El-Sayed answered. "Obviously, I don't want to do anything that drives your fear. At the end of the day, there's a difference between safety, or lack of safety, and comfort. If what I'm saying is making you uncomfortable, you should be uncomfortable with injustice perpetrated on other people. You should be uncomfortable with that. I don't want anything we do to make anybody unsafe, to put them in harm's way." He continued, "But addressing the safety question and the discomfort question are two different things. Because if it is your sense of your discomfort and/or fear of safety that has to keep me quiet while I watch 70,000 people get killed, their homes annihilated, their hospitals destroyed, their universities decimated, and I can't critique that, then I think what you're telling me is that their humanity matters less than yours, and I'm not going to be OK with that." ABDUL EL-SAYED HITS BACK AT ISRAEL QUESTIONS, SUGGESTS HIS NAME AND FAITH ARE BEHIND PRESS SCRUTINY When asked what he believes Israel should be as a nation, El-Sayed answered that the country should uphold "equal rights" but appeared to take issue with the nation being associated solely with the Jewish faith. "I believe that Israel ought to be a country that upholds equal rights for all of its citizens, equal rights for all its citizens, does not identify itself with a culture or a faith, and that dignifies the rights of those citizens to live free under its laws. That’s, again, the question of peace, dignity and self-determination," El-Sayed said. NANCY PELOSI CALLS MAMDANI, EL-SAYED'S PAST COMMENTS ON ISRAEL 'CONCERNING' AND 'WRONG' Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's team for comment. El-Sayed has been criticized for his past views on Israel, particularly his hesitation to answer whether he believes Israel has a right to exist. Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, condemned El-Sayed's comments as "outrageous and hateful" and accused him of criticizing efforts to fight Hamas, the terrorist organization. articles.title: In 2023, Australia placed a 13-tonne octopus sculpture eight metres underwater to create habitat; it joined a sculpture trail where marine life began settling by the January 2024 opening
articles.summary: Discover the innovative Underwater Sculpture Park in Busselton, Australia, featuring Ophelia the Octopus and 12 other sculptures designed to enhance marine habitats and attract diverse marine life.
articles.body: An artwork placed beneath the sea has a different audience from its counterparts in a gallery. Its surroundings change, its surface weathers, and its appearance can shift as marine life develops. At Busselton Jetty, the sculptures were designed with that process in mind. Busselton Jetty noted snorkellers at the late-January 2024 opening could already see organisms settling on the works. They were initially placed around the jetty’s submerged piles in the previous winter.Ophelia the octopusAccording to the Busselton Jetty, one of the largest additions was Ophelia the octopus, a 13-tonne concrete figure by South-West artist Brendan Booth. It was placed under the sea at the Busselton Jetty as part of a 13-sculpture series.Ophelia was made from a high-sulphate-resistant concrete and composite mix. It was then reinforced with glass-fibre concrete. To cope with its weight, the octopus was built in five different sections. More than 80 stones set into the sculpture are designed to absorb sunlight during the day and glow after dark.Booth had worked in Western Australia’s South-West for more than 25 years, the Busselton Jetty noted. He was responsible for creating the Margaret River Sculpture Park and Wood Be Good Woodcraft Gallery, a sculpture park that featured carvings in wood, stone and other materials. His other work included furniture and homewares from local Western Australian hardwoods.Art meets artificial reefOphelia was one of the 13 sculptures produced by 12 Western Australian artists for the Busselton Jetty Underwater Sculpture Park and Artificial Reef Project. The works varied in size, from 2 by 2 metres to 10 by 6 metres. Artists used materials such as steel, ceramics, bronze and marine-grade concrete. According to a Divernet report in 2024, the sculptures were installed in June and July 2023, during the period when the Leeuwin Current flowed south towards Busselton and Geographe Bay.The materials did not acquire growth at the same rate. The mild-steel works were fitted with zinc anodes to curb corrosion, Divernet reported. The installation sat among the submerged supports of Busselton Jetty, a timber-piled structure built in 1865. The jetty extends 1.84 kilometres out to sea and is described by Divernet as the longest timber-piled pier in the Southern Hemisphere. Its piles have developed into an artificial reef that supports 300 marine species, including marine invertebrates, the Busselton Jetty noted.The sculpture project added hard surfaces to part of Geographe Bay where this kind of habitat was uncommon. Busselton Jetty said each work was meant to function as an artificial reef and to create places for marine organisms to settle. The Busselton Jetty Environment Foundation took charge of monitoring colonisation at the park.Plunging in: visitor access and park rules According to Divernet, the jetty is operated by Busselton Jetty Inc., the non-profit organisation that directs 25% of the revenue into maintenance and repairs. Other revenue came from dive and snorkel passes for visitors who wanted to view the sculptures.Visitors reach the park from one of three ladders on the Universal Access Platform on the jetty’s western side. The jetty operator noted that under the right weather, seven of the 13 sculptures could be spotted from the jetty’s decking. However, the works escape view from inside the Underwater Observatory, where the tour focused on the natural marine environment.According to Busselton Jetty, the dive or snorkel pass costs $5, and before visitors entered the water, they must complete a waiver in person at the Interpretive Center. A waterproof map priced at $15 shows the locations of all 13 sculptures, while guided tours are given by Swan Dive Busselton.Another activity permitted to visitors was scuba diving, but fishing and collection are prohibited. A separate 20-metre exclusion zone surrounds the Underwater Observatory. Swimmers are instructed to remain on the ocean side of the western access, at least two rows of jetty piles from the underwater building.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Iowa residents near ammunition plant told to vacate before Army detonates 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
articles.summary: The Army asked Middletown, Iowa, residents to temporarily evacuate Friday before it detonates 68 drums of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
articles.body: The Army is asking residents of a southeast Iowa town to temporarily evacuate Friday as it plans to detonate five tons of a bomb-making chemical that it says has turned into an "explosive safety hazard" after being "deemed unsafe for relocation." It warned that the detonation of the 68 drums of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown "will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground." Lead azide is a chemical that is used to set off munitions. "While safety measures will be fully enforced, the controlled detonation will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead," according to the Army. "Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and see a plume of dust which is expected to linger for no more than one hour after the detonation, depending on wind speed." Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the track of the plume, prompting a notification to communities as far as 100 miles away. CRIMINAL PAST OF ILLINOIS ETHANOL PLANT BOMB SCARE SUSPECT INCLUDES MULTIPLE FELONIES, 2 PRISON STINTS Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered. "The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable," Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time. The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. On Nov. 13, the Environmental Protection Agency approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday's detonation. "EPA issued the Emergency Permit based upon the determination that the explosion risk from the degraded condition of the lead azide presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment," the EPA said. "The Army has provided EPA information documenting that recrystallization of the lead azide in long-term storage has occurred. The recrystallization of lead azide has created a risk of spontaneous explosion due to the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation," according to the EPA. LIVE WWII-ERA GRENADES TURN UP IN UNLIKELY PLACE; BOMB SQUAD WARNS OF DANGER "The Army, which has unparalleled expertise in matters concerning explosives safety, concluded that this material cannot safely be handled or moved and therefore, cannot be treated by any method other than in-place detonation," it also said. The Army said that the lead azide barrels "will be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with Hesco barriers full of sand which are approximately two stories high." Residents of Middletown are being advised to leave their homes between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. local time Friday. Officials also have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north toward other communities. Some schools in the path of the plume have canceled classes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Before and during the detonation, the soil above the earth-covered magazines will be thoroughly saturated with water, and water misters will be spraying. These measures should reduce the amount of lead that migrates from the detonation through the air off the installation," the Army said. "Extensive modeling efforts predict that the potential level of lead particles in the air may be elevated but well below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Putin pitches Arctic route, calls for investment: Will it work?
articles.summary: Analysts say some Asian investors may show interest, but the route is unlikely to be a viable global shipping lane.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has used his speech at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit to pitch investments in the country’s Arctic regions, as Moscow hopes to spearhead year-round navigation on the Northern Sea Route (NSR), which is currently confined to the summer months.

“I am confident that the business community and investors from APEC economies will fully appreciate the opportunities emerging in the Russian market – and, naturally, will take advantage of them,” Putin said on Wednesday in Shenzhen, China, according to Russian media.

The package proposed by the Russian president to support this includes tax breaks on profits, property and land, as well as reduced payroll contributions and preferential leases, Russian media reported.

His APEC speech follows Putin’s remarks at the Eastern Economic Forum in the Russian city of Vladivostok in September, when he also outlined plans to make navigation along the NSR year-round as well as to introduce new measures to expand transport, energy and technological infrastructure.

Russia has been developing the Arctic shipping corridor which connects its northern ports to the Pacific region. But Putin’s efforts to turn the NSR into an important artery of global trade have raised concerns about geopolitical and security challenges, as well as environmental risks for the fragile Arctic environment.

What is the Arctic route and why is Russia betting on it?

The Arctic shipping lane runs for about 5,600km (3,480 miles) along Russia’s northern coast, from the Novaya Zemlya archipelago in the west to the Bering Strait in the east. But it is only navigable for a few weeks of the year when the ice melts during the summer.

A more reliable shipping route through the Arctic could ease global trade, which is currently hampered by the Middle East crisis that has paralysed critical waterways, including the Bab al-Mandeb strait on the edge of the Red Sea, which feeds into the Suez Canal, and the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Shipping companies have become increasingly interested in alternative trade routes amid these heightened security concerns.

China announced its own new shipping route through the Arctic Ocean in August, dubbed the “ Ice Silk Road ”, which also takes in Russia’s NSR.

Climate change, which has contributed to major melting in the Arctic, is making the route more navigable for longer stretches of the year, raising its prospects as a viable alternative to existing shipping corridors.

The layer of frozen seawater that caps the Arctic Ocean, which melts through the summer to its annual low in September, has reached record lows. This year, according to NASA, it shrank to its lowest on satellite record.

Can Putin succeed in turning the Russian Arctic into a global trade route?

It might be trickier than it seems. While a changing climate is slowly transforming the Arctic, experts say the region remains largely impervious.

“Harsh climate, low visibility, short windows of navigation opportunities, drifting ice will remain serious obstacles for a large-scale commercial traffic,” Andrey Todorov, a researcher at the Netherlands Institute for the Law of the Sea (NILOS), told Al Jazeera.

“Any serious consideration of shipping through NSR will require not only investing in ice-capable vessels, which will be not as efficient and commercially viable in non-polar waters, but also experienced and knowledgeable masters, crew and operators.”

Todorov said he expects navigation along this route to remain “very niche and limited”, serving mainly Russia’s goal of transporting mineral resources extracted in the Arctic to the world market. At most, the analyst predicted, “a very small portion of transit container traffic, on a scale far from comparable to that of the traditional southern routes”.

Ksenia Vakhrusheva, Arctic project adviser at the Bellona Environmental Transparency Center in Vilnius, Lithuania, said Putin has been seeking to attract Chinese investments in the Arctic because Moscow doesn’t have the financial resources to carry the project through.

European sanctions on Russia’s energy sector have made it more urgent for Moscow to ship oil and gas to Asian markets through alternative shipping lanes, as Russian and Ukrainian forces target cargo ships in the Black Sea.

While China has been keen to “keep an eye” on the Arctic, Vakhrusheva said turning the NSR into a global maritime trade route does not appear realistic. “Everyone understands that route is under full control of Russia,” she said. “I don’t think that other players, including China, want to be dependent on a single country.”

Pavel Devyatkin, senior associate and leadership group member at The Arctic Institute, however, said he is confident that Asia-Pacific partners like China, Japan and South Korea would take up Putin’s call to increase participation and further route development.

“At the same time, the concerns are real: there is limited search-and-rescue capacity, environmental risks from heavier traffic, and the danger of the Arctic being drawn into geopolitical confrontation,” he said.

What could opening up the Northern Sea Route mean for the Arctic?

From an environmental point of view, more shipping could increase black carbon emissions and exacerbate the effects of climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss in the fragile Arctic.

A 2024 review by the Ocean & Coastal Management journal on the impact of Arctic shipping on the region’s environment showed a negative impact on water bodies, air emissions and wildlife.

The melting ice is also exposing a new geopolitical fault line.

Much of the NSR runs through Russia’s economic zone, where it regulates navigation. Russia and China are strengthening cooperation to develop the route, while United States President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that Washington must take over Greenland to prevent Moscow and Beijing from dominating the Arctic. In September, the US, Denmark and Greenland signed a deal on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, granting Washington a greater military presence on the continent-sized Arctic island.

Trump’s repeated threats to take over the Danish territory in the lead-up to that have strained US relations with European allies.

articles.title: As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
articles.summary: The UK premier is heading to Brussels for the second round of EU talks aimed at deepening post-Brexit cooperation.
articles.body:
Lincolnshire, United Kingdom – A decade is a short time in cheesemaking. Barrels of Tim Jones’ “Lincolnshire Poachers” cheese rest on their racks for months and years, disturbed only by Florence, the robot cheese turner.

Complexity, depth and flavour develop with patience.

The most mature cheese in Tim’s Lincolnshire dairy, in the English midlands, is five years old. By that measure, it was only a couple of cheeses ago that 52 percent of the British public voted for the country’s most tumultuous constitutional revolt in living memory.

Jones was one of them. But he is under no illusion that it went well – particularly for his exports.

“It suddenly made life much harder. We lost certain customers, and it became more expensive to get the cheese there. It definitely harmed our business,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ten years after the UK voted to leave the European Union, few are happy with what they got.

Remainers are still heartbroken that a majority of the country did not look on EU membership with approval. Leavers, by and large, think many of Brexit’s promised benefits were never delivered.

“I did vote to leave,” said Jones. “But I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did.”

Recent polling tells a consistent story: A majority of Britons now view Brexit as a mistake.

In September, 55 percent of respondents told YouGov that leaving the EU was a wrong turn for the UK. Only 21 percent think it was the right decision.

Fifty-nine percent of Britons now support rejoining the EU.

The relatively new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has noticed the shift in public mood. Less cautious than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Burnham reignited the Brexit debate shortly after taking office in July.

He has ruled out major changes to the UK’s relationship with the EU before the next general election. But he would like to see the country back in the bloc within his lifetime, and has suggested that a future Labour manifesto could promise a new referendum.

The changing mood is only part of the logic. A government searching for growth would naturally prioritise what is still its biggest trade partner. Geopolitics matter too. The UK’s bond with the United States is less reliable than it was.

Unsurprisingly, Brexit talk has swept through media in Britain and, to a lesser extent, in Europe. Burnham insists he will not get ahead of the public on this. His immediate concern, he says, is improving the current UK-EU relationship.

On Friday, Burnham will be in Brussels for the second UK-EU Summit – a vehicle established under Starmer to deepen post-Brexit cooperation.

Among the deals being worked on are a youth mobility scheme, an emissions trading agreement, and a food and drink trade deal.

Jones, the Lincolnshire cheesemaker, is hopeful.

“If he can reduce the red tape and the cost of sending cheese to Europe – and for us that means across the world – that would be a huge positive for us,” he said – although he was less certain which way he would vote in another referendum.

“Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. I think it would depend entirely on a critical view on the arguments that were presented at the time. A much more critical view than I had the first time around.”

It is an issue familiar to anyone who has lived through the Brexit years: the terms matter.

Former premier Theresa May used the motto, “Brexit means Brexit”. But the slogan was vague. What kind of Brexit? Hard? Soft? Norway Plus? Canada Plus?

There were many potential Brexits – as there might be many possible ways to rejoin.

A new YouGov survey gave people a menu of 18 options.

In the most popular scenario, 58 percent said they would vote to rejoin if the UK stayed out of the euro, joined the border-free Schengen Zone, and kept its previous rebate from the EU budget. But if the UK lost the rebate, did not join Schengen, and adopted the euro, only 35 percent of people said they would be interested in EU membership.

Anticipating the battles ahead, two pro-Brexit campaign groups are relaunching under new names: Stay Out and Enough Official.

Burnham says he will begin talks with the EU about options for the long-term relationship after this week’s summit.

Buckle up, the Brexit wars may be starting again.

articles.title: Palestinians flee and Gaza ceasefire tested as Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’
articles.summary: Israel’s ground operation across the yellow ceasefire line in Gaza, which forced Palestinians to flee their makeshift shelters, marks a fresh escalation in the conflict and risks undermining an already floundering truce with Hamas, analysts said Thursday.
articles.body: Israel’s ground operation across the yellow ceasefire line in Gaza, which forced Palestinians to flee their makeshift shelters, marks a fresh escalation in the conflict and risks undermining an already floundering truce with Hamas, analysts said Thursday. As tanks rolled into central Gaza on Wednesday, residents could be seen carrying blankets and other belongings away from their tents in pictures and video taken shortly after the Israeli military began what it said was an operation targeting a “terror tunnel.” Others could be seen rolling away mattresses on carts and pushing loved ones in wheelchairs away from the scene near the Nuseirat camp in central Gaza. At least one person was reported to have been killed in an Israeli airstrike near the raid, Palestinian medics said, according to Reuters. “Bullets were fired at us,” Amna al-Gasar, 49, told NBC News after she fled the scene with her young children, her baby in a pink fluffy sweater strapped to her chest. She said her family had received “evacuation orders” from the Israeli military and that tanks had advanced on the area. “This is the 14th time that we’re getting displaced,” al-Gasar said, who added that she is from Gaza City in the north of the enclave which is now on the side of the “yellow line” occupied by Israeli forces. “Where should we go? We are exhausted. This is not a life,” she said. Muna Abu Shehadeh, 37, said in a separate interview that along with some of her relatives, she left “with nothing but our children — no bedding, no food, and no water.” She added that she had a daughter who was ill, as well as a baby, and that they had to leave behind what few supplies they had. The Israeli military told NBC News the ground operation was the first to be executed beyond the yellow line — the boundary marking the roughly 60% of Gaza that remains occupied by Israeli forces — since the U.S.-brokered ceasefire with Hamas came into effect in October 2025. Separately, in a joint statement with the Israel Security Agency, or Shin Bet, the Israel Defense Forces said the operation was a “targeted” assault aimed at dismantling a tunnel that “posed an immediate and direct threat” to troops. They said a warning had been issued to civilians in the area prior to the operation, though they did not expand on how exactly warnings were issued and whether they expanded beyond an announcement published online, when asked by NBC News. Israeli forces would continue to operate to “remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts” by Hamas to harm Israeli civilians or troops, the statement added. A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Thursday that the operation west of the yellow line had “ended,” though they could not confirm when exactly the offensive came to a close. Hamas condemned the ground operation, calling it a violation of the ceasefire agreement. Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at King’s College London’s School of Security Studies, said he also believed the incursion was a “clear violation of the fundamental premise of the ceasefire.” “Israel agreed to withdraw to the ‘yellow line,’ which was supposed to establish a mutually understood boundary until further withdrawals could be negotiated,” he said Thursday. Sending ground forces a few hundred feet beyond that line and “forcing civilians to flee undermines the agreement,” he added. “Israel cannot simply invoke security concerns whenever it wants to cross a boundary it agreed to respect,” he said, adding that its assertion of a threat had “not been independently substantiated.” The operation risked undermining “any meaning” the yellow line has held as a boundary under the ceasefire agreement, he said. The Israeli government and military did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the accusation that the ceasefire agreement had been violated. The truce has already been marked by regular Israeli strikes, with more than 1,600 people killed in the enclave since the truce began, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the territory. Israel says at least five soldiers have been killed within the same amount of time, according to Reuters. Both Israel and Hamas have repeatedly traded accusations of ceasefire violations. “Israel has been violating the ceasefire pretty periodically since it came into place, so it’s nothing new on that front,” Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in defense studies at King’s College London, said Thursday of the Israeli military’s ground operation. “It’s the scale of the violation,” he said, adding the ground assault and use of tanks signifying an “escalation” from Israel. Both Pinfold and Krieg noted that the ground operation comes at a time of great political uncertainty for Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces losing his prime ministership after elections last month. While Netanyahu’s Likud party gained the most votes, President Isaac Herzog tasked his main rival, Gadi Eiskenot, with forming a coalition government based on the premise that he was most likely to succeed in doing so. Netanyahu has railed against the possibility of Israel’s Arab-led parties joining a coalition and both Pinfold and Krieg suggested that he might be seeking to ramp up pressure around security concerns. Pinfold said Netanyahu was also likely “trying to see how far he can go on the Gaza front,” particularly as the U.S. continues to sideline Israeli involvement in the war with Iran. “I suspect Israel is testing how far it can push the Americans without provoking a serious response,” Krieg said. Israel could also be seeking to “establish a precedent for what amounts to a permanent right of hot pursuit” in Gaza, even beyond its current “yellow line” and even into the future as efforts to advance the peace continue to stall, he added. Elsewhere, President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, the body that is overseeing the execution of the U.S.-brokered ceasefire, delivered a bleak report Tuesday on its progress to the United Nations Security Council, warning that the fragile deal was in danger of collapse, Reuters reported. The board said both Israel and Hamas should uphold the commitments made in the agreement, according to Reuters, which obtained a copy of the report. But Hamas’ disarmament and the militant group’s calls for the Israeli military’s withdrawal from Gaza have proven major sticking points in efforts to propel the deal forward. Fleeing from the area of Israel’s ground operation Wednesday, al-Gasar said Palestinians “need a solution.” “All we ask for is safety and security. We’re not asking for a lot,” she said. “All of this talk in the media about advancement in negotiations, but instead we find advancement of tanks.”

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Thursday hit back at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his remarks to industry leaders at the annual general meeting of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) in New Delhi, accusing him of failing to address economic problems created by his own government.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the Prime Minister had echoed concerns long raised by the opposition, including stagnant wages, weak private investment and inadequate job creation.In a post on X, he said: "For the first time in 12 years, a nervous and rattled PM has pulled up the captains of industry."His remarks came after PM Modi questioned corporate leaders over inadequate salary hikes and job creation despite several government concessions. Taking a swipe at India Inc, the prime minister said, "How much ever you give, their [India Inc] appetite is never satisfied."Reacting to the remarks, Ramesh said PM Modi had acknowledged three concerns repeatedly raised by the Congress, "wages have not increased; tax rates have been cut, but investment has not boomed; and obs are simply not expanding at the desired rate."The Congress leader also claimed that industry representatives would have been surprised by the prime minister's remarks."The captains of industry must have been taken aback and shocked. They would not have expected this lament and to listen to the PM in this RAGA," he said.However, Ramesh argued that the prime minister could not distance himself from the economic situation and held his government's policies responsible for the challenges facing businesses and workers.He accused the government of allowing an "unprecedented concentration of economic power" across industries, saying oligopolies were weakening competition. He also alleged that an atmosphere of fear and intimidation had hurt investor sentiment.Ramesh further accused the government of allowing regulatory institutions to be captured by a select few and using investigative agencies to favour one conglomerateAlso check: 'Bhookh itni hai, pet bharta hi nhi': PM Modi pulls up industrialists over lack of jobs, low pay despite tax cutsOn trade and taxation, he blamed the government for the widening trade deficit with China, which he said had hurt lakhs of micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). He also criticised demonetisation and the Goods and Services Tax (GST), describing the latter as "cumbersome and complicated"."The list can be expanded," Ramesh said, urging Modi to stop complaining and take responsibility for the economic situation.He alleged that the government's policies and style of functioning had contributed to high inflation, weak job creation and subdued private investment."The PM should stop complaining. He should look inwards and accept that both the substance and style of his governance have been such that inflation is raging, job growth is not happening, and private investment continues to be tepid," he said."Industry demands and deserves better," he wrote.The statement follows PM Modi's remarks at the FICCI gathering questioning whether they had increased employee salaries or expanded their workforce after the government reduced corporate tax rates, simplified tax procedures and cut GST rates on several products."I have given income tax relief up to Rs 12 lakh. But have you increased the salaries of your employees? Have you increased the number of employees? No! It is always: 'Modi ji, you do it; we will see what happens.' articles.title: Pennsylvania investigated Walmart after reports of underage workers being injured and found repeated breaches of child labour rules; the retailer has agreed to pay $7.8 million and change its practices
articles.summary: Walmart has agreed to pay nearly $7.8 million to settle a Pennsylvania investigation that uncovered repeated violations of child labour laws at its stores
articles.body: Walmart has agreed to pay nearly $7.8 million to settle a Pennsylvania investigation that uncovered repeated violations of child labour laws at its stores across the state. The investigation began after reports of underage employees being injured while working at Walmart locations, prompting state officials to examine the retailer's employment practices. Investigators subsequently identified violations involving excessive working hours, missing work permits and failure to provide legally required breaks to young employees.According to an announcement published by the Pennsylvania Department of Labor and Industry on November 9, 2026, the settlement is the largest child labour enforcement action in the state's history. The agreement requires Walmart to pay financial penalties and introduce additional measures to ensure compliance with laws protecting young workers. The state said the investigation revealed a pattern of violations that extended beyond the stores initially examined.How Pennsylvania's investigation into Walmart beganThe Department of Labor and Industry's Bureau of Labor Law Compliance began investigating Walmart in February 2025 after receiving referrals from the department's Bureau of Workers' Compensation. The referrals concerned minors who had been injured while working at Walmart stores. Investigators conducted 10 audits at eight Walmart locations across Pennsylvania. The inspections uncovered an average of 65 violations of the state's Child Labor Act per audit. After identifying repeated breaches, officials expanded their enforcement efforts beyond the stores initially investigated and pursued a settlement covering Walmart locations throughout the state.The violations included failure to obtain the required work permits for minor employees and failure to notify school districts when young workers were hired or had their employment terminated. Investigators also found that some minors were not receiving the breaks required under state law and had been allowed to work more hours than legally permitted.Pennsylvania's Child Labor Act regulates the employment of minors to protect their health, safety and welfare. It places restrictions on working hours, prohibits young employees from undertaking certain types of work and establishes requirements for permits and workplace conditions.Walmart agrees to pay $7.8 million in penaltiesUnder the settlement, Walmart will pay $7.68 million in administrative penalties. This amount is in addition to $142,785 in fines the retailer had already paid following the department's initial investigations. Together, the payments amount to approximately $7.8 million. The Shapiro administration described the agreement as the largest child labour settlement in Pennsylvania's history and one of the largest enforcement actions of its kind by a state labour agency in the United States.Governor Josh Shapiro said the settlement reflected his administration's commitment to protecting workers and enforcing employment laws. He warned employers against taking advantage of young workers and said businesses would be expected to follow the rules designed to protect them.Pennsylvania Department of Labor and Industry Secretary Nancy A. Walker said the investigation had revealed a pattern of violations that required action beyond the individual stores initially audited. She said the settlement would help hold Walmart accountable across the state and introduce measures to prevent similar problems in the future.New compliance measures Walmart must followThe financial penalties are only one part of the agreement. Walmart has also committed to introducing changes to its workplace practices to reduce the risk of further child labour violations. Under the settlement, managers will receive training on Pennsylvania's child labour laws. The company must also display workplace notices informing employees about their rights and the protections available under the state's Child Labor Act.Walmart will be required to provide employment records concerning minor workers at selected locations at six-month and one-year intervals following the execution date of the settlement agreement. These records will allow state officials to monitor the company's compliance with the rules. The agreement also includes a stricter financial consequence for future breaches. If violations are identified during the compliance checks specified in the settlement, Walmart will face an amplified penalty amounting to twice the department's typical fine figure.These requirements are intended to ensure that the retailer follows the state's employment protections not only at the locations initially investigated but also across its wider Pennsylvania operations.Pennsylvania's wider child labour enforcement effortsThe Department of Labor and Industry said it had investigated more than 2,200 child labour cases since Governor Shapiro took office in January 2023 and had identified violations by hundreds of employers.The Walmart agreement represents a significant enforcement action, combining financial penalties with additional monitoring and workplace requirements. For young employees, the measures are intended to strengthen protections relating to working hours, breaks, employment documentation and other conditions governed by Pennsylvania law.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rare rhino's first steps at Chester Zoo captured on video
articles.summary: Zookeepers say the rhino's birth is a "special moment" for the under-threat one horned species.
articles.body:
The moment a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros took its first steps at a zoo has been captured on video.

The calf was born at Chester Zoo in Cheshire this week.

The video shows 19-year-old mother Asha with her newborn calf at their enclosure after Asha had been pregnant for 15 months.

Keepers said both rhinos were in good health and the birth was an important step in the conservation of the threatened species.

Tom Garland from the rhino team at Chester Zoo said the calf was the fourth born to Asha and father Beni, who died earlier this year following a short and sudden illness.

"It's always exciting to welcome a new calf and Asha has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters," he said.

"Every birth is important for the future of this species and it's wonderful to see another healthy arrival."

The species was driven to near-extinction in the early 1900s by habitat loss and trophy hunting and remains vulnerable to extinction with around 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos living in the wetlands, forests and grasslands of India and Nepal.

The calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding programme that helps to maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos in human care.

Conservation scientist John O'Hanlan said supporting Asha's 15-month pregnancy had been "really exciting".

"She's one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population," he said.

Mark Brayshaw, Head of Mammals at Chester Zoo, said in addition to safeguarding the genetics of the species, Asha and her calf could also help millions of zoo visitors understand the value of conservation.

"Greater one-horned rhinos are much better protected in the wild than they once were, but many of them are concentrated within one national park in India, which makes them vulnerable to illness and environmental changes," he said.

"They still need people to love and protect them."

articles.title: Don't buy smart glasses, Dutch data watchdog advises
articles.summary: Tests of glasses showed some misread medicine instructions or pretended to have called an ambulance
articles.body:
The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.

While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.

The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent , or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.

Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.

It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.

The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.

Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.

Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.

The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.

But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.

AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.

It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.

One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.

The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.

And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.

It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.

Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.

It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.

In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses

Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI .

It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.

The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.

In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument around smart glasses.

"They can help me and others better understand our surroundings, access information and navigate the world with greater confidence," he wrote in September.

But he said he had been "shocked and appalled by some of the irresponsible and harmful ways people are using these technologies".

articles.title: FCC gives state prisons the go-ahead to jam signals from contraband cellphones
articles.summary: COLUMBIA, S.C. — The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday acted to allow state prisons across the United States to jam the signals of cellphones smuggled to inmates as the federal government cracks down on devices that authorities say are the No. 1 security threat in the nation’s correctional facilities.
articles.body: COLUMBIA, S.C. — The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday acted to allow state prisons across the United States to jam the signals of cellphones smuggled to inmates as the federal government cracks down on devices that authorities say are the No. 1 security threat in the nation’s correctional facilities. The vote was unanimous among the commissioners meeting in Washington. State prison officials for years have sought the right to jam, arguing that blocking the signals of contraband phones would halt inmates’ ability to use the devices to run drug rings, coordinate prison riots and even order acts of violence such as attacks on guards. Under the new rule, prisons are not required to use the jamming technology, they must conduct multiple tests to make sure cell signals outside prisons are not affected and they have to notify officials if the jamming devices are moved. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who spoke in favor of the measure, visited this week with officials in South Carolina, whose prison directors have led efforts to obtain permission to jam. Cellphones have been smuggled inside hollowed-out footballs, whisked in by corrupt employees and sometimes even dropped by drone. The signal-jamming technology was already allowed in federal facilities but needed FCC permission, due to a nearly century-old communications law, to be available for state prisons. U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling, who headed South Carolina’s Corrections Department for more than a decade, led an effort from many of his counterparts across the country to gain use of the technology. South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson, elected this month as the state’s next governor, organized fellow prosecutors to press Congress to change the law but they were unsuccessful. FCC chair says it’s ‘ready to take action’ While in South Carolina, Carr stood alongside Stirling, Wilson and other South Carolina officials before a display of hundreds of confiscated cellphones and massive drones used to ferry the contraband over prison fencing. He said many people might not perceive the danger. “People really don’t understand the threat that these pose,” Carr said, noting that 25,000 cellphones were confiscated in the nation’s state and local prisons each year. “We’re going to put a new tool in the hands of law enforcement, and it’s going to make a dramatic difference.” Carr cited the case of Robert Johnson, a South Carolina corrections officer who was nearly killed at his home in 2010 in a hit that officials said was orchestrated by a prisoner using a contraband cellphone. After nearly three dozen surgeries and now in “pain 24/7,” Johnson said Wednesday that he refers to the phones as “weapons of mass destruction” because of the potential dangers for which they can be used. He has testified in previous FCC hearings over jamming requests and often spoken out on the issue. “No one should have to go through what I went through,” Johnson said. “But I also believe that the Lord chose my wife and I to go through this because someone had to carry the banner, and he chose us to do it.” South Carolina tested the tech in 2008 South Carolina has been the testing ground for state prison cellphone jamming. In 2008, the FCC allowed the state to conduct a one-time test of a jamming system at a maximum-security prison. A briefcase-sized device emitted a frequency that immediately shut down cellphones around an auditorium; outside, service was uninterrupted. Another test took place at a different state prison in 2019, a first-time collaboration between federal officials and state prison officials. A year earlier, seven South Carolina inmates had died in the worst U.S. prison riot in 25 years, in what officials said was a gang fight arranged in part using illegal cellphones. The FCC has shown willingness to work on eradicating prison cellphones, holding a 2016 field hearing in South Carolina and hosting meetings with members of Congress, prison officials and representatives of the wireless industry. Groups that advocate for inmates’ rights have opposed the move, arguing that the high rates inmates must pay to use official prison phones have pushed them toward using contraband cellphones just to stay in touch with family. The telecommunications industry has long argued against it, too, saying that jamming technology risks interfering with legitimate communications. Carr said in South Carolina that he felt the industry was softening on jamming, in part due to recognition of the problem’s size as well as agencies’ experiments with targeted technologies. “We aren’t considering jamming outside this unique context,” Carr said. “Maybe people aren’t cheering it on from industry, but the opposition has receded substantially.” ___ Meg Kinnard can be reached at

articles.title: Iraq reaches compromise with Kataib Hezbollah over armed group’s stronghold
articles.summary: The compromise reached will unite forces that include brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces.
articles.body:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says his country’s security forces will establish a joint operations centre in the town of Jurf al-Sakhar, in a compromise with the Iranian-backed Kataib Hezbollah armed group over control of a strategic area south of Baghdad.

The Jurf al-Sakhar area has long been a stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah, and the new agreement comes after the Iraqi government announced plans to send in security forces amid allegations that the group was smuggling oil.

The compromise reached late on Thursday will see a new combined force deployed to the area, consisting of a brigade from the Iraqi army, a brigade from the Federal Police, a regiment from the Energy Police to provide protection for oil pipelines in the area, and two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are officially part of Iraq’s security forces, including some Kataib Hezbollah fighters.

A military spokesman said the new joint operations centre will open at 6am local time (03:00 GMT) on Friday morning.

In a statement, the PMF said their forces will begin replacing the military units stationed in Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, in accordance with the directives from Prime Minister al-Zaidi.

Earlier in the week, an Iraqi official told Al Jazeera that the commander of the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, arrived in Iraq to push for a solution due to the simmering tensions with Iran.

A Kataib Hezbollah spokesman confirmed that Qaani met with senior members of their organisation, as well as the head of PMF and a representative from the Badr Organization, an Iranian-backed political group that also contributes armed fighters to the PMF.

In a statement, Kataib Hezbollah said the talks addressed the current crisis and described the outcomes of the discussions as positive.

Separately, in a news conference on Thursday, Kataib Hezbollah expressed appreciation for the PMF and Iraqi security forces for preventing escalating tensions that serve “the enemies”. The group also affirmed that any existing issues would be resolved through private channels.

A senior Iraqi official previously told Al Jazeera that Kataib Hezbollah had until Friday to leave Jurf al-Sakhar. The group had threatened to confront government troops and had rejected the government’s efforts to disarm non-state militias.

articles.title: Palestinians in Gaza face new displacement after Israeli army operation
articles.summary: Families in Nuseirat spend the night without shelter, while many fear returning despite Israel ending offensive.
articles.body:
Nuseirat, Gaza Strip – For the 13th time, Suhail al-Mashharawi has been forced to flee. The 50-year-old Palestinian and his family of eight spent the night in a schoolyard in central Gaza, without blankets, bedding or enough clothing to protect his children from the cold.

Thousands of Palestinians have once again been forced to abandon their makeshift shelters as Israeli forces launched a major ground operation in the enclave, the first major offensive publicly announced by the military since a ceasefire was agreed in October 2025.

On Wednesday, the Israeli military issued forced evacuation orders covering three blocks north of the Nuseirat refugee camp, saying its troops were targeting a suspected Hamas tunnel.

The military announced on Thursday that it had completed its operation and reopened Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south thoroughfare.

While some Palestinians began returning to check on their belongings, others stayed away, saying that sporadic gunfire continued and the road remained unsafe.

For al-Mashharawi, the operation ended a year of relative stability, forcing him and his family to abandon their tent and seek refuge at a nearby educational centre.

He described the conditions there as “dire”, saying his family had received no humanitarian assistance and had no idea how long they would have to stay.

About 6,000 Palestinians fled the area on Wednesday, Gaza’s Government Media Office said.

Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that threatened its troops. Hamas condemned the incursion as a violation of the ceasefire, while the Israeli military accused the group of violating the agreement.

More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health authorities.

About 1.4 million Palestinians across Gaza now live in tents or makeshift shelters, according to United Nations humanitarian figures.

Ismail Younis, who manages a camp for displaced people in the al-Mufti area, said bullets penetrated the tents during the operation, with a quadcopter flying over the camp, prompting families to flee quickly.

“The families left without having a specific destination, or an alternative place for them to take refuge,” he said. “Their main concern was to save their lives and the lives of their children, in light of the escalating gunfire and continued shelling.”

Amna al-Qassas, 49, was one of those who had to rapidly flee her camp in Nuseirat when the forced evacuation came. She had time to pack only a small bag containing her family’s identification documents.

Al-Qassas fled with 10 family members, leaving behind the tent and possessions she had managed to salvage during an earlier displacement from the Tuffah neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City.

She told Al Jazeera that displacement had become a “recurring nightmare”, taking her family back to square one and destroying what little sense of security they had regained.

Now, they were being forced to leave again. “We have not had time to think … our only concern was to escape death, even if it meant fleeing into the unknown,” she said.

Unable to find a vehicle to transport her belongings, al-Qassas left everything behind. She fears the destruction of her shelter could leave her with nothing to return to.

articles.title: World reacts to ICJ finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary: Landmark judgement in The Hague is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.
articles.body:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.

The landmark judgement in The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.

The case filed by Gambia in 2019 has been closely watched by governments, lawyers, rights groups and Rohingya communities for its implications for how states are judged under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The court said Myanmar has an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations ‌it committed, with the terms to be determined at a later date.

Here’s how key parties and world leaders reacted to the landmark verdict:

Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government

The National Unity Government, which includes remnants of former leader Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party, said it respects the authority of the International Court of Justice and its judgement.

It pledged to consider the court’s findings and orders, reaffirming its commitment to accountability and preventing further atrocities.

The Gambia, which brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the support of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, welcomed the ruling with “profound satisfaction”, calling it “a historic day for international justice”.

The government said the obligation to prevent and punish genocide is shared by all states party to the 1948 Genocide Convention and called on Myanmar to comply with the judgement “fully and without delay”.

In a post shared on X, the OIC commended the ICJ’s judgement, saying it offered “redress for victims and [upholds] the principle of no impunity”.

Antonio Guterres described the ruling as a “demonstration of international justice” and a reaffirmation that impunity for “such horrific acts must not stand”.

He noted that it marked the first time the court had found a state responsible for committing genocide and called on Myanmar to comply with its decision.

Volker Turk said the judgement “clearly concludes” that Myanmar is responsible for “one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind.”

In a post shared on X, he added that the Rohingya people’s “suffering is a stain” on humanity.

Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache and summoned the country’s charge d’affaires. He also called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the ruling.

He said further measures would be announced in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held accountable.

Yanghee Lee called it a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.

Rohingya activist and co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council

Activist Nay San Lwin said justice for the Rohingya means the restoration of their citizenship, recognition of their identity and their safe and dignified return home.

He added that their struggle would continue until those demands are met.

Rohingya activist and executive director of Women’s Peace Network

Activist Wai Wai Nu said the ruling had shattered the military’s decades-long efforts to erase Rohingya identity, deny their existence and dismiss their suffering.

“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and ⁠compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.

The human rights group said the ruling was a “historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”.

Human Rights Watch senior international justice counsel

Maria Elena Vignoli welcomed the court’s decision, calling it a “long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military”.

articles.title: European leaders unite in Berlin to reaffirm support for Ukraine
articles.summary: German chancellor warns peace talks without Europe’s involvement are doomed to fail, urging unity with Ukraine.
articles.body:
European leaders of the so-called “Coalition of the Willing” gathered in the German capital for talks intended to signal a united front in support of Ukraine.

The Berlin meeting happened hours after an unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.

Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the Shenzhen meeting a “photo op”, warning that any deal made without Europe at the table would fail.

Merz said that “if it comes to peace negotiations, then we will be involved”, adding that such talks “can only be successful with Ukraine and Europe”.

Merz said he hoped to work as a “team with Kyiv and Washington” when they hold talks with Russia on ending the Ukraine war, although no announcement of when that would be has been made.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe is “ready to enter negotiations”, insisting that “a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia must come first”.

“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,” Burnham added.

European countries have been angered after the European Union was largely sidelined in the United States’ stop-start negotiations with Russia and Ukraine.

However, Donald Trump’s son-in-law and peace envoy Jared Kushner said, “Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side.”

Kushner said, “We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war.”

The British prime minister welcomed the US presence at talks in Berlin, saying it added momentum to end the war.

“This clearly has got to be a moment ⁠to move towards ⁠peace because of the US involvement that we’ve ⁠seen today and ⁠the progress clearly ⁠that is being made,” Burnham said.

Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to ramp up efforts to end the war.

“Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.

“Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said. NATO membership for Ukraine is among the issues holding back a peace deal for Ukraine.

In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, “We do not want Russia to drag all of this out into the winter. Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia.”
