articles.title: HC greenlights Gaggal airport expansion, says serves larger public interest
articles.summary: Himachal Pradesh HC clears Rs 4,064-crore Gaggal (Kangra) airport expansion, upholds land acquisition, cites IAF strategic value; orders fast TEFR and EIA.
articles.body: Shimla: The Himachal Pradesh high court has cleared the proposed Rs 4,064-crore expansion of Kangra airport at Gaggal, holding that the project serves a larger public interest and land acquisition is inevitable despite its social costs and citing its strategic value to the Indian Air Force.A division bench comprising Justice Vivek Singh Thakur and Justice Ranjan Sharma disposed of a petition filed by the Gaggal Airport Expansion Affected Social Welfare Committee challenging the July 7, 2023, land acquisition notification and the social impact assessment (SIA) report.The bench observed that although the committee lacked legal standing to maintain the petition, the court examined the merits and found no grounds to intervene. It held that the right to residence and livelihood under Article 21 cannot override acquisitions in the larger public interest.Dismissing objections over the Kangra region’s earthquake vulnerability, the court observed that the airport is already operational and pointed to Bhuj airport in Gujarat, which functions safely despite being in a high-risk seismic zone.On the demand for alternative sites, the court said the proposal concerned expansion of the airport and not construction of a new one.The Airports Authority of India (AAI) had explained that alternative alignments were technically unsuitable and would require costly bridges over river channels. The multi-disciplinary expert group had concluded that no less-displacing viable option was available. Rejecting allegations of irregularities in the SIA process, the court said there was no material to establish that the assessment team’s alleged visits to the project site before formal issuance of the notification had violated the law. It also noted that the committee had failed to demonstrate any prejudice caused by these visits. The SIA report had subsequently been completed through a survey and public hearings following public notices.Despite greenlighting the project, the court warned the state govt against risking public funds without securing mandatory approvals. It noted that more than Rs 460 crore had already been disbursed under land acquisition awards and thousands of crores were likely to be spent. The court directed the state to complete the techno-economic feasibility report (TEFR) at the earliest and immediately initiate steps for environmental clearances under the Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 2006, without waiting for completion of the acquisition process. It emphasised that project work could commence only after obtaining the necessary environmental clearances.As per the techno-economic feasibility report (TEFR), the cost of the expansion of Gaggal airport has been worked out to be Rs 4,064 crore.Gaggal Airport’s ImportanceThere are three airports in Himachal — Bhuntar (Kullu), which has been operational since 1956 and was metalled in 1967; one in Shimla, operational since 1987; and Kangra airport at Gaggal, operational since 1989. Kangra airport has the largest runway length of 1372×30 metres, which is suitable for landing 72-seater aircraft with load penalty. At present, an ATR-42 aircraft is operating from this airport with load penalty. Airports Authority of India has stated that only Kangra Airport is suitable for expansion but . articles.title: Jeremy Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
articles.summary: Lawyers will study the way in which Gambia proved the crucial point that Myanmar intended to commit genocide, writes the BBC's international editor.
articles.body:
This judgement that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people is historic. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The Rohingyas are getting justice that is long overdue. At least 10,000 were killed when their communities were attacked by Myanmar's security forces and local militias in 2017.

In the huge camps in Bangladesh where more than one million Rohingya refugees have been living since they fled the terrible events of 2017, crowds gathered around screens to watch the President of the ICJ, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, deliver the court's verdict.

He recalled some of the evidence heard by the court since the Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It described acts of mass murder, rape, torture and the destruction of villages, sometimes with Rohingya residents burnt to death inside their homes.

Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules

The decision by a majority of nine votes to six at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will also have a significant impact on the other genocide cases currently being heard by the court by reasserting and clarifying the standard of evidence needed to prove genocidal intent.

They include South Africa's case that Israel committed genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza in its response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Israel has repeatedly and vehemently denied the allegation.

The court's landmark decision also reinforces those who believe in the rules that were made to regulate the way that power is wielded after World War Two. The 1948 Genocide Convention was a vital part of the structure that was built around the United Nations to stop a repeat of the unfettered brutality, war and genocide in the years before the defeat of the Nazis.

The rules and conventions established after 1945 have been under unprecedented pressure in the era of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. On the day of their summit in China, the ICJ issued a reminder that international law still exists and perhaps can show that the use of force against civilians has consequences.

Lawyers will study the way in which the Gambia proved the crucial point that the state of Myanmar intended to commit genocide.

Proving intent is the biggest challenge in a genocide case at the ICJ. Showing that atrocities occurred is not in itself enough.

The key phrase from the Genocide Convention, adopted by the United Nations after the Nazi Holocaust of European Jewry, defines the crime as "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national ethnical, racial or religious group".

The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.

That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.

In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.

Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.

According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent.

"The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."

In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.

The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.

The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".

The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide.

"If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over.

"But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."

The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.

The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.

That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.

The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".

It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.

Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.

Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".

Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.

He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.

She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

But whatever the threats coming from the Trump Administration, it is clear that delivering justice to the Rohingya people will refocus attention on Israel's conduct in Gaza, South Africa's case at the ICJ and on the continuing plight of Palestinians in the ruins of Gaza, where more than 1,400 have been killed by Israel since the ceasefire just over a year ago.

It would be wrong, lawyers say, to view the Myanmar case as a dress rehearsal for the case against Israel.

"It risks distracting from the Rohingya, who should appropriately be our focus," according to Janina Dill, from Oxford University.

"Litigation on their plight is not a test case for a conflict that the world has chosen to pay more attention to."

Millions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?

articles.title: Simon Harris wants border poll criteria talks with London
articles.summary: Simon Harris says a conversation between the British and Irish governments over the criteria for a border poll would be "useful".
articles.body:
The tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minister) has said that a conversation between the British and Irish governments over the criteria for a border poll would be "useful".

Simon Harris said he and the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin are "aligned" on the issue.

Adding that it "would be useful at a point in time to understand the criteria that a British government may consider applying to decide whether or not to call a border poll".

It comes after the Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said that it is his job to decide when to bring forward a border poll and that he does not "detect a mood" for it.

Harris said that it would be good if the the British and Irish governments "could at least have a shared understanding as to what criteria may be considered".

"At a point in time Dublin and London having a conversation about criteria is useful and is also just good governance," he said

Speaking on BBC News NI's The View programme, he added: "British Irish relations have never been better".

Under the Good Friday Agreement, Bryant as the NI Secretary of State, decides whether to call a border poll or not.

On Thursday morning Sir Chris told RTÉ's Morning Ireland programme he would "only bring forward a border poll at such time" as he thinks the people of Northern Ireland would want to join a united Ireland

"I don't detect that that is the situation now," he added.

Asked what criteria he will use to decide if the mood to join a united Ireland appears likely, he said "when it appears likely".

When asked why the Irish government should not have a role, Sir Chris said that the Good Friday Agreement is very clear that it's a matter for the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and that is agreed by the two governments as co-guarantors.

In response, the tánaiste said that "the commitment in the Good Friday Agreement is exactly as Chris Bryant read out, there's no disputing of that. But the application of that is something that would be good to have a greater understanding".

Simon Harris sent a letter to some party leaders in Northern Ireland asking for their views after his party, Fine Gael, published proposals on how to prepare for Irish unity .

The "blueprint" on Irish unity came days after the taoiseach, leader of Fianna Fáil, circulated a document to his parliamentary party laying out his own thoughts on how to prepare for a united Ireland .

He proposed setting up a new "initiative" on the constitutional future of the island of Ireland.

The two parties are both in a coalition government, supported by a number of Independent TDs (members of the Irish parliament) in Dublin.

Simon Harris is due to become taoiseach in November 2027, under the coalition's rotating taoiseach agreement.

Among their proposals, Fine Gael has suggested appointing a junior minister in the Irish government for "north south relations".

The party also published a document by an economist who works as an adviser to Harris, where it was suggested that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about €3bn (£2.5bn) to €25bn (£20.8) to the Irish exchequer.

His party has now proposed setting up an "independent, government-supported, inter-party and consultative forum" as part of preparations for reunification of the island.

The forum would look at the "future" of the institutions in Northern Ireland and the "possible subsequent reform of local and regional government on an all-island basis in line with the European principle of subsidiarity".

It would also examine the changes needed in Ireland's institutions, as well as public taxation, healthcare, education and other public services and practical requirements.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that his party was "not interested in self-harm and conversations that would see the end of the UK as we know it".

Speaking on the Nolan show , he said that it should be "no surprise to Simon Harris or anyone else that the Democratic Unionist Party, unionists like me, we have absolutely no interest in a discussion about the destruction of our own country".

Alliance leader Naomi Long has said that her party will "engage respectfully" in any conversations about Northern Ireland's future.

Speaking on Sunday Politics , Long said Alliance would take part "without prejudice to how we might decide the constitutional question".

The SDLP leader Claire Hanna welcomed the letter and said "a New Ireland must mean precisely that: an opportunity to build a new nation, not simply reverse partition".

"Crucially, that preparation must also deliver a better Northern Ireland along the way, with stronger public services, greater economic opportunity and better living standards for communities," she added.

The leader of the UUP, Jon Burrows, called Fine Gael's plans a "constitutional pet project" and said that his party "will not participate in any project designed to dismantle the United Kingdom".

"We have no interest in a republican invitation to commit political suicide."

In his response to Harris, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said his "courtship techniques are somewhat lacking".

"My message to you is simple: you run your part of this island as your people wish, but butt out of the affairs and future of those pleased to be part of a larger and more prosperous United Kingdom, upon whose defence capacity you are glad to rely," he added.

articles.title: Demolition at iconic filmmaker Ritwik Ghatak’s ancestral home in Rajshahi sparks outrage. Cultural activists & film enthusiasts demand preservation of  site
articles.summary: Outrage erupts over alleged damage to Ritwik Ghatak’s ancestral home in Rajshahi, Bangladesh; activists seek preservation as officials dispute fresh demolition.
articles.body: Kolkata: The alleged demolition of a wall at iconic filmmaker Ritwik Ghatak’s ancestral home in Bangladesh—alongside the felling of an adjacent banyan tree—on Tuesday has sparked outrage, with cultural activists and film enthusiasts on both sides of the border demanding the immediate preservation of the historic site. Activists claim there have been repeated attempts to raze the house in Rajshahi’s Miyanpara since 2024.The incident comes amid unrest in Bangladesh ahead of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s return.However, Bangladesh’s deputy high commissioner to India, Mohammed Khaled, told TOI that the wall had collapsed in 2024 and no fresh demolition was carried out. “In 2024, authorities of the Rajshahi Homoeopathic Medical College, which operates out of the premises, felled a banyan tree. The wall broke down then and was never repaired,” Khaled said.Although Ghatak was born in Dhaka in 1925, his family soon moved to Rajshahi when his father was posted there as a district magistrate. The Miyanpara residence has long served as a pilgrimage site for the filmmaker’s admirers. While the front portion of the property later housed the homoeopathic college, the rear section preserved a hand-pump and the rooms once occupied by Ghatak and his family.Mahmud Hossain Masud, general secretary of the Rajshahi-based Ritwik Ghatak Film Society, told TOI that the organisation had proposed in 2017 to convert the building into a heritage site housing a ‘Ritwik Centre’ for screenings and workshops.“We met then-deputy commissioner Abdul Jalil in 2020 to urge him to preserve the historic building, and an ad-hoc committee was formed to verify the plot’s ownership,” Masud said. “It was found that the land is still registered in the name of Ghatak’s mother, Indubala Debi. It was merely leased out to the Rajshahi Homoeopathic Medical College and Hospital authorities during former President Hussain Muhammad Ershad’s regime. College authorities cannot simply claim ownership and start demolishing it this way.”Following an assessment, the public works department was tasked with conserving the site. “A budget of over 51 lakh Bangladeshi Taka was earmarked for the work. However, despite our repeated requests, the funds were never released,” Masud added. Three rooms of the building were subsequently demolished in Aug 2024, following the fall of the Hasina govt. After widespread protests, college authorities had allegedly promised to halt further razing.On Nov 4 this year, the Ritwik Ghatak Film Society was forced to observe the filmmaker’s 101st birth anniversary amid the rubble.Premendra Mazumder, vice-president of the Federation of Film Societies of India, said, “The fact that the land is still registered in Ghatak’s mother’s name gives us even stronger grounds to demand its preservation. We strongly condemn these repeated attacks on his ancestral home.”Meanwhile, The Daily Star reported that Naharul Islam, additional deputy commissioner (education and ICT) and chairman of the college’s governing body, confirmed he had heard about the recent damage. Islam stated that college authorities told him routine cleaning work might have inadvertently caused the collapse, adding that all work has since been halted.Ghatak scholar Sanjay Mukhopadhyay recalled visiting the house about five years ago. “It was a pilgrimage for me. This is a terrible tragedy and a crime against history. Ritwik Ghatak is an icon of modern cinema, and his ancestral home is an inseparable part of Bengali modernity,” he said.Filmmaker Anup Singh—whose film Ekti Nadir Naam follows characters reminiscent of Ghatak’s cinema crossing fractured landscapes—reflected on the loss: “Ghatak knew well enough the fragility of any home in this world, and how easily walls crumble when power decides that its citizen is a foreigner. There is a sad irony in the unmaking of the house of a man whose whole life was forged out of ruin.”The only assurance, Singh offers, is Ghatak’s voice was “never enclosed within those Rajshahi or any other brick walls”.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: In West Virginia, furious citizens and energy companies square off over data centers
articles.summary: West Virginia residents say the Valley Link Transmission Project could seize property through eminent domain to send electricity to data centers.
articles.body: A scene playing out across the country unfolded in Ranson, West Virginia, Wednesday night as opponents of the Valley Link Transmission Project showed up en masse to an open house run by the companies behind it, demanding to be heard. The proposed power line would cut a swath through the Mountain State to send electricity to data centers in Northern Virginia, opponents claim. But those gathered argued that the end does not justify the means, particularly the seizure of private property through eminent domain. When I asked Dan McGinn, a native West Virginian, why he was there, he told Fox News Digital that he and other Jefferson County residents received "a flyer in the mail, just a flyer in the mail, telling you they’re going to take your property." WEST VIRGINIA LOOKS TO AI DATA CENTER BOOM TO HELP ELIMINATE STATE INCOME TAX When pressed for details on this unfortunate postal delivery, McGinn said it was "just a cheap flyer, nothing personal, no details, just a line on a map saying they are going to take your property." Melissa Hope was also among those organizing the protest at the open house, complete with the "BBQ and Cupcakes" promised on the flyers that were ubiquitous in the county. "I’m near the lines but not directly in the path of the lines," the sixth-generation farm owner told Fox News Digital. "Since we’ve learned of this, I’ve spent pretty much the past four or five months now just trying to share the word." THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO Hope is concerned about more than the property rights of her friends and neighbors, though. "We are going to bear the cost of these lines, but no benefit," she said, "especially in Jefferson County. Our history and our beauty are part of our economy." Outside the civic center stood a crane draped in a banner, illustrating the 180-foot height the transmission lines would reach, dwarfing every building in Ranson and nearby Charles Town. Both cities have seen enormous growth in housing stock in recent years, only adding to concerns about strains on resources and infrastructure. INSIDE THE NEIGHBORHOOD LIVING ON THE EDGE OF AMERICA’S TECH FRONTIER I caught up with Valley Link spokesperson Lauren Siburkis amid the clamor, and she told Fox News Digital that, before Wednesday, more than 7,000 people had offered input, and their feedback had been taken into account. She said the open house was "a second look for residents in the community to take a look at where the proposed routes could go … so that when we go back to the drawing board to put together a final route, we make sure that all of the community input is factored in." As sincere as Siburkis was, the assembled property owners remained skeptical but were also realistic about the need for power and data centers. McGinn pointed out that the objectors held differing views. "We have pro-data center people and anti-data center people, pro-power line people and anti-power line people … but this power line is indefensible," McGinn said. DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS Danny Lutz, the conservation district supervisor of Jefferson County, went so far as to express doubts about whether the power was really needed, arguing it is "a long-term solution to a short-term problem." Lutz was referring to initiatives like Google’s Project Suncatcher, which would effectively put data centers in space. His words do bring to mind the giant, ugly-as-sin windmills — many nonfunctional — that scar the Appalachian highways of Maryland and Pennsylvania. Nobody wants an ugly power line to nowhere, after all. Military experts often talk about the difference between the map and the ground. For example, on D-Day, the map showed a clear path for tanks to Germany, but on the ground there were obstacles the map couldn’t show. The data center debate raging in our society is very similar. NEIGHBORHOOD BACKLASH COLLIDES WITH AMERICA'S TECH ARMS RACE — BUT IS THIS THE PLAN TO FIX IT? From 30,000 feet, it is utterly obvious that we need more data centers to power our phones and keep us ahead of China on artificial intelligence. But nobody lives 30,000 feet in the air. On the ground, Americans refuse to be bulldozed, literally or figuratively. Valley Link will almost certainly get its power line in some form eventually, but the company was wise to hold the open house, one of several across the affected counties. What the people want, more than anything else in this age of lightning-fast technological change, is just some say over it, and the right to fight for their own property. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There are many issues in American political life that are black and white. Data centers and power lines are not among them. Instead, all sides present legitimate competing interests. On Wednesday night at the Ranson Civic Center, the warring parties were at least in dialogue.

articles.title: A customer bought a discounted Best Buy open-box television labelled 'Excellent' for around $600, but its screen did not work; the retailer refused the return, and a federal court allowed parts of the lawsuit to proceed
articles.summary: A customer who paid roughly $600 for a Best Buy open-box television labelled ‘Excellent’ received a set whose screen did not work, only to have the
articles.body: A customer who paid roughly $600 for a Best Buy open-box television labelled ‘Excellent’ received a set whose screen did not work, only to have the retailer refuse the return. The dispute has reached court, where a judge has allowed parts of her lawsuit to proceed. Sylvia Kemigisa bought the television in June 2022 through Best Buy’s Open Box programme, but it arrived wrapped in plastic and displayed coloured lines instead of a picture. The court said she may pursue claims concerning the packaging and return policy, while dismissing her consumer fraud claim without prejudice and allowing her to amend it.Best Buy’s Open Box programme and ‘Excellent’ condition promiseAccording to the court, Best Buy’s Open Box programme allows customers to purchase previously returned products at discounted prices. The retailer categorises these items as ‘Excellent’, ‘Satisfactory’ or ‘Fair’, depending on their condition.Best Buy describes products in ‘Excellent’ condition as items that “look brand new—with no physical flaws, scratches or scuffs—and include all original parts and accessories (or a suitable replacement).” The retailer also states that such products will arrive in their original packaging or a suitable replacement.Kemigisa purchased an open-box television on June 13, 2022, which was listed as being in ‘Excellent’ condition. She received it the following day, but it arrived wrapped in plastic rather than its original packaging.When she attempted to switch it on, the television did not work. The court document records her description of the fault: “the screen displayed lines of different colours, and there was no picture displayed.”Best Buy disputed the return, claiming the open-box TV had a cracked screenOn June 20, 2022, Kemigisa’s nephew, Fesali Kaidi, took the television back to the Best Buy store where it had been purchased. However, the retailer allegedly refused to accept it. According to the court filing, Best Buy employees “refused to accept the television with no explanation and ordered Mr Kaidi out of the store.” Kaidi interpreted their conduct as being motivated by his race.Later that month, the plaintiffs contacted Best Buy through legal representatives in an attempt to explain the situation and reach an amicable resolution. However, Best Buy responded in a letter dated August 19, 2022, denying their allegations. The retailer said it had refused the return because there was a crack in the television screen.Kemigisa and Kaidi disputed that explanation, maintaining that the screen had never been cracked and describing Best Buy’s reason for refusing the return as a lie. Best Buy’s return policy, as outlined in the court document, allows customers to return products, including Open Box purchases, within 15 days of delivery, provided they are in a like-new condition. It also states that returns may be refused for items that are damaged, unsanitary, dented, scratched or missing major contents.Judge rejects Best Buy’s arguments over faulty TV packaging and return policyThe plaintiffs initially filed their lawsuit in the Circuit Court of Cook County on December 1, 2022. Kemigisa brought claims for breach of contract and violations of the Illinois Consumer Fraud Act, while Kaidi pursued a claim under the Illinois Human Rights Act.After Best Buy transferred the case to federal court, the plaintiffs sought permission to amend their complaint and introduce class-action allegations. Their proposed amended complaint sought to represent customers nationwide who had purchased faulty Open Box products and had been unable to return them.The proposed claims included breach of contract, breach of implied warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose, and violations of the Illinois Consumer Fraud Act.In its June 9, 2026, decision, the court said Best Buy had acknowledged that Kemigisa had stated a valid breach of contract claim based on the allegation that the television was not working when sold. The retailer nevertheless argued that she could not pursue claims based on the packaging or return policy because its policies had not been violated.Judge John J. Tharp Jr. rejected that argument at this stage of the proceedings, stating that the court would not conclude that the plastic bag in which the television arrived was a “suitable replacement”. The judge also declined to determine that Best Buy had complied with its return policy, explaining that whether it had done so was “a key factual dispute in this case”. The decision therefore allowed Kemigisa to continue pursuing her claims based on either the packaging or the retailer’s return policy.Judge questions Best Buy’s alleged faulty product schemeThe court also examined Kemigisa’s allegation that Best Buy operated a wider scheme through its Open Box programme, selling defective products while misrepresenting their condition and subsequently refusing returns when customers discovered the faults. She alleged that the retailer promoted the programme through misleading representations on its website, social media and other advertisements.The judge acknowledged that these allegations went beyond an ordinary breach of contract and could potentially support a claim under the Illinois Consumer Fraud Act if backed by sufficient factual details.However, the court found that Kemigisa had not provided enough specific information to establish the alleged nationwide scheme. It also highlighted inconsistencies between her claims that Best Buy operated an institutional policy of refusing returns and her separate allegation that employees had rejected her nephew’s return because of racial animus. The opinion stated that she needed to provide more facts supporting the existence of the alleged scheme and clarify its nature.Court dismisses nephew’s claims but keeps TV dispute aliveAs a result, the judge dismissed her Illinois Consumer Fraud Act claim without prejudice, meaning she could attempt to bring it again with a more detailed complaint. The court granted her permission to amend the claim by June 30, 2026.Kaidi’s claims were dismissed with prejudice because he had not purchased the television himself and therefore could not pursue the contract, implied warranty or consumer fraud claims brought in the amended complaint.In its concluding order, the court stated that Best Buy’s motion to dismiss was denied insofar as it sought to prevent Kemigisa from pursuing arguments concerning the television’s packaging and the retailer’s return policy. The motion was granted with prejudice as to Kaidi’s claims and without prejudice as to Kemigisa’s consumer fraud claim.The judge also denied Best Buy’s motion to strike the class-action allegations without prejudice, following the decision to allow the amended complaint.Disclaimer: This article is based on information contained in publicly available court records. The allegations concerning Best Buy’s refusal to accept the television’s return, the condition of the screen and the retailer’s Open Box programme have not been independently verified. The court’s decision does not establish Best Buy’s liability or confirm the alleged nationwide scheme. All claims should be understood in the context of the ongoing legal proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
